## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, use `list_tables` to understand the existing structure
- When debugging issues, start with `get_logs` and `get_advisors` before making changes
- Use `get_project_url` and `get_publishable_api_key` when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Use `apply_migration` carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

One server-side answer to "what may this user do?". ### The tier model was DECIDED this session, and MONETISATION.md was amended **`MONETISATION.md` contradicted itself.** §1 said the daily drop must never be gated; §2 counted drops toward a limit of 3/day — with drops counted, a free user who viewed three occasions is refused the fourth, which *is* gating the drop. §1 matches Decision 4 in `CLAUDE.md`, so §2 gave. The doc now carries the amendment inline with the reasoning; `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` had the correct model all along. **The model as built (user decisions, 2026-08-04):** | | Free | Pro | |---|---|---| | An occasion's first look of the day | free, all 4 occasions | free | | Regenerate | **1 per occasion per day** | unlimited | | Style a look around a piece | **gated** | unlimited | | New pieces added | **10 per day** (a RATE, not a closet cap) | unlimited | | Re-opening anything already generated | free | free | Free ceiling = 4 drops + 4 regenerates = **8/day ≈ $0.72/user/month**, realistically ~$0.20. - **Per-occasion beats a global daily number.** A global meter is a wallet the user watches draining and can block an occasion they have not looked at yet. It was also blind to styled looks in both directions while styling was already gated. The ledger is append-only with `kind: 'drop'|'regenerate'|'styled'` — the `kind` fix that #8 and #11 both already called for. 2. **`Entitlements` has no `generationsPerDay`.** Replaced by `regeneratesPerOccasion`, `styledLooks` and `uploadsPerDay`. 3. **`profiles.tier` is revoked from `authenticated` NOW**, not deferred to billing. RLS scopes rows, not columns, so the existing self-update policy would otherwise let any user run `update profiles set tier='pro'` from the browser. ### ⚠️ `server-only` is installed and is load-bearing — never drop it to fix a test Not a Next dependency; it is React's, and Next's docs tell you to install it. Now the limited state keeps the look and the takeover only renders when there is genuinely nothing to show. 2. **The styled gate's copy was false.** It read *"that's today's stylings used — back tomorrow"* (PR #22, written when styling was assumed to share the daily allowance). Styling is a capability, so tomorrow gives a free user no more of them. **The Pro gate is a sheet, not a caption** (user, 2026-08-04): a small muted line under the primary button read as a validation error rather than a feature you have not bought, and offered no way forward. `components/billing/upgrade-sheet.tsx` is shared, because five surfaces are gated. **The gated control stays live and tappable** — nobody buys a feature they have never reached for, so the sheet is the answer to the tap, not a fence around it. No checkout exists yet; it closes with "Got it" and the profile hub's Pro card (queue #9) becomes the real destination. **Local DB was modified by verification:** `generation_events` has 3 rows (drop/regenerate/styled for `work`, 2026-08-04), today's `work` drop was regenerated once, and a styled outfit exists for the Karl Lagerfeld dress shirt. ` it was also clipped by that element's `overflow-hidden`, so its colour palette and "Show N looks" button were unreachable. ""` in `app/outfits/[id]/page.tsx:61` — deferred by user decision 2026-08-03: **"fix only after shipping whole app"**, i.e. no standalone bug-fix PRs until the feature queue is done. 161

163	
164	| Pattern | How it works |
165	|---|---|
166	| **Brand kicker** | Uppercase, letterspaced, muted, tiny — sits *above* the title (`HARTLEY`). Wayfinding, never content. |
167	| **Serif display title** | Libre Caslon Text, large, cream. The name of the thing (`Pale Blue Oxford`). |
168	| **Grotesk subtitle** | Hanken Grotesk, muted, `·` as the separator (`Oxford shirt · Pale blue`). |
169	| **Stat tiles** | A row of 3 rounded surfaces: serif value on top, uppercase micro-label under it (`30 / TIMES WORN`). The row is the screen's "how you actually wear it" summary. |
170	| **Labelled meter** | Uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right (`FORMALITY … Smart casual`), then 5 segments with the filled ones in rust. Never a number on its own — always the word. |
171	| **Spec table** | Hairline-divided rows, muted label left, cream value right. Multi-values joined with `·` (`Spring · Autumn · Winter`). |
172	| **Horizontal card row** | Uppercase kicker (`GOES WITH`) over a scrolling row of cutout cards with a caption under each. |
173	| **Bottom action bar** | One small secondary icon button + one full-width cream pill for the single primary action (`Style an outfit with this`). One primary action per screen. |

176	quiet around them**, and **the rust accent appears exactly once** (the meter) — the One Rust Rule in

178

180	`item-data-completeness`, for cost/wear) and wear logging (queue #4 `outfit-detail-wear-logging`, for
181	times-worn and last-worn). That is why #5 sits behind them. And `Style an outfit with this` is still an
182	**open decision** — see "Open decisions blocking a plan" above; it conflicts with Decision 5.

### ⚠️ Settings (#9b): do NOT ship "Auto-log worn looks" as written

The plan specifies *"when on, opening a look after 18:00 local logs it."* **Rejected — opening a look is
not wearing it.** `wear_logs` is the foundation of cost-per-wear, streaks, most-worn, gathering-dust and
gap analysis, i.e. of everything Pro sells. Logging views as wears inflates all of it permanently, with
no way afterwards to tell a fabricated wear from a real one — poisoning the paid feature to save one tap.
`MONETISATION.md` §1: *"they pay for it in month three, once the data is theirs."*

**Build an evening confirmation instead** (agreed with the user 2026-08-05): if you opened a look today
and logged nothing, ask once — *"Did you wear <look> today?"* — **Yes / No**. Yes writes the same row the
button writes; No writes nothing and it does not ask again that day. Triggers when the app is next opened
after ~18:00 local, so it needs no web-push and is buildable now.

Two details that decide whether it helps or hurts: **Yes and No must be equally easy** (a lone "Yes" with
a dismiss ✕ gets tapped to clear it, and the data inflates anyway), and it asks only about looks actually
opened, most recent first — dwell time is not tracked, so "most recent" is the honest simple choice.

It is **bigger than a toggle**, so it wants its own small plan. Settings then ships **rain guard as its
only live toggle** — which is that plan's own stated rule: *"rendering a switch that schedules nothing is
the lie this plan is trying to avoid."*

**Price/copy decisions already applied in #27** (kept here for the record): the price is **€5**, not the
design's £5 — the app targets the EU and every other price renders in euro. The feature list still ships
verbatim, **packing mode included**, which is deliberate while nothing can be bought; it must be built
before Pro is actually sold, or dropped from the copy then.

## The end-of-build design audit (#16)

**User request, 2026-07-28:** after all `todo/` plans *and* the `scoping/` items are implemented, do a
full design review/audit of the product using **`impeccable`** and **`design-taste-frontend`**.

- **`impeccable` is the primary tool** — it is already configured for this repo (`.impeccable/live/config.json`)
  and reads `DESIGN.md` / `PRODUCT.md`, so it audits against *our* system ("The Midnight Atelier"), not a
  generic one. `/impeccable audit <surface>` per screen, then `polish`.
- **`design-taste-frontend` is a partial fit** — it is written for landing pages, portfolios and
  redesigns. Its audit-first redesign mode applies; its landing-page defaults do not. Fitcheck is a
  mobile-only PWA. Use it as a second opinion on "does this look templated", not as the system of record.
- **Judge at phone width, in the iOS Simulator** — never a resized desktop browser. A desktop-width
  screenshot has already produced false findings on this project once (see the occasion-row measurements
  in `docs/STATE.md`).
- **Sequencing caveat:** `scoping/2026-07-24-womens-wardrobe-scoping.md` adds one-piece garments
  (dresses/jumpsuits), which changes the flat-lay layout templates and the credits list. Auditing the
  visual system *before* that fork lands means auditing it twice. If the women's fork stays deferred
  ("a lot later"), run the audit on the menswear product and re-run the affected screens afterwards.
- Two known items are already parked for this pass: the **10–11px uppercase kickers** (deferred by
  decision 2026-07-24, see below) and the **off-ramp font sizes** the impeccable hook flags in
  `refine-sheet.tsx` / `stylist-view.tsx` / `item-card.tsx`.
- Existing drift is catalogued in `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` — read it first so the audit does
  not rediscover what is already written down.

## Open decisions blocking a plan

- ~~**"Style an outfit with this"**~~ — **CLOSED 2026-07-30, shipped in PR #22.** None of the three
  options as posed: it pins the piece, generates once, and **caches the answer** by
  `(user, item, local day)`, so a second tap that day is a free read (measured 9.7s → 256ms). Decision 5
  forbids paying twice for a question already answered — styling a chosen piece is a *different*
  question, so it gets its own cached answer rather than an exemption. The filter-today's-looks reading
  was measured and rejected: only 62% of the closet appears in today's looks even on a heavy day, so ~3
  taps in 4 generated anyway *and* discarded the result. Rationale in
  `done/2026-07-24-item-detail-rebuild.md`; remaining quality gaps in `todo/2026-07-31-styled-look-depth.md`.
- **Wear Stats gap analysis** — *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* is a simulation of what a hypothetical item
  would enable, not a query. Needs designing.
- **"See curated picks"** (`:767`) — a commerce/affiliate surface with no product decision behind it.
- **Small type** — the design uses 10–11px for its uppercase kickers, which our design-system guide
  flags. **Deferred to the end of the project** by decision on 2026-07-24; do not spend time on it.

## Not in the queue

- `scoping/2026-07-24-womens-wardrobe-scoping.md` — the one-piece-garment (dress/jumpsuit) fork.
  Deliberately deferred: "womens a lot later".
- `scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md` — a Pro feature the design names and specifies nowhere.
  Deferred 2026-07-24 pending a discussion of its seven open decisions.
- `scoping/2026-07-24-stylist-chat-scoping.md` — tell the stylist about today, or a special occasion
  ("wedding", "client meeting") the four fixed occasions cannot express. Deferred 2026-07-24. **The
  headline decision is one-shot intent capture vs. an actual conversation** — the first is one
  structured call that reuses everything we have; the second is a new architecture and the most
  expensive thing in the product.
- The occasion learner — waiting on real `occasion_overrides` data.

Both scoping docs list the decisions that must be made before a plan can be written. A plan written from
either one as it stands would be rewritten.

### Unblocking them visually — `imagegen-frontend-mobile`

**Added 2026-07-28.** The three scoping docs above, plus "See curated picks" and the wear-stats gap
analysis, are all blocked on the same thing: **a screen nobody has designed.** `Fitcheck.dc.html`
specifies twelve screens and none of them is packing mode or the stylist chat, so the decisions get
argued in the abstract.

Use the **`imagegen-frontend-mobile`** skill to generate concepts for those screens *before* writing
their plans. It produces images inside phone mockups and touches no code, so it is cheap and reversible
— and a picture makes "one-shot intent capture vs. an actual conversation" a decision you can look at
rather than imagine.

**Every generated concept must inherit the item-detail language** (see below). Generating in a different
visual register is worse than not generating — it produces something attractive that we then cannot
build, and the drift catalogued in `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` started exactly that way.

## Source of truth for anything visual

`design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html` — the complete twelve-screen design, verified
against the Claude Design project *Styling* on 2026-07-24. Two identical copies also exist at
`styling/project/Fitcheck.dc.html` and inside the design-handoff folder. `docs/STATE.md` previously
described this file as a duplicate to ignore; that was wrong and is the root cause of the drift
catalogued in `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md`.

### The canonical screen: item detail (`Fitcheck.dc.html:587-657`)

**User decision, 2026-07-28: "we should still follow this detail page for cloth, it's the best."** When
a new screen has no design of its own — a generated concept, a Pro feature, an empty state — derive it
from this one. It is the most complete expression of the system, and the plan that builds it is queue #5
(`2026-07-24-item-detail-rebuild.md`).

The reusable vocabulary, in the order the screen uses it:

| Pattern | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Brand kicker** | Uppercase, letterspaced, muted, tiny — sits *above* the title (`HARTLEY`). Wayfinding, never content. |
| **Serif display title** | Libre Caslon Text, large, cream. The name of the thing (`Pale Blue Oxford`). |
| **Grotesk subtitle** | Hanken Grotesk, muted, `·` as the separator (`Oxford shirt · Pale blue`). |
| **Stat tiles** | A row of 3 rounded surfaces: serif value on top, uppercase micro-label under it (`30 / TIMES WORN`). The row is the screen's "how you actually wear it" summary. |
| **Labelled meter** | Uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right (`FORMALITY … Smart casual`), then 5 segments with the filled ones in rust. Never a number on its own — always the word. |
| **Spec table** | Hairline-divided rows, muted label left, cream value right. Multi-values joined with `·` (`Spring · Autumn · Winter`). |
| **Horizontal card row** | Uppercase kicker (`GOES WITH`) over a scrolling row of cutout cards with a caption under each. |
| **Bottom action bar** | One small secondary icon button + one full-width cream pill for the single primary action (`Style an outfit with this`). One primary action per screen. |

Two things this screen encodes that are easy to lose: **cutouts are the hero and everything else is
quiet around them**, and **the rust accent appears exactly once** (the meter) — the One Rust Rule in
`DESIGN.md`. A concept with two rust elements is already off-system.

Note the dependency chain this screen implies: its stat tiles need price (queue #3
`item-data-completeness`, for cost/wear) and wear logging (queue #4 `outfit-detail-wear-logging`, for
times-worn and last-worn). That is why #5 sits behind them. And `Style an outfit with this` is still an
**open decision** — see "Open decisions blocking a plan" above; it conflicts with Decision 5.

Result: once the API key is set, **every capture fails at the tagging step, always.** **Fix:** use the SDK's Zod helper — it strips unsupported constraints before sending and validates the response against the Zod schema (also replaces the hand-rolled `parseTagText` in `lib/ai/parse-tags.ts`): ```ts import { zodOutputFormat } from "@anthropic-ai/sdk/helpers/zod"; const res = await client.messages.parse({ model: "claude-haiku-4-5", max_tokens: 512, output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(TagSchema) }, messages: [ /* unchanged */ ], }); const tags = res.parsed_output; // already validated Tags | null — guard for null ``` --- ### 2. Server Action payload exceeds Next's 1 MB body limit for typical photos **Where:** `components/capture/capture-flow.tsx:45` (+ `next.config.ts` sets no override) **Bug:** `uploadAndTag` sends **two base64 images** in one Server Action body. The compressed original is up to 0.5 MB (≈0.67 MB as base64); the @imgly cutout is a 1280px PNG **with alpha and no size cap** — routinely 0.5–3 MB (+33 % base64). Combined payload exceeds the default `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` of 1 MB → `"Body exceeded 1 MB limit"` → "Capture failed" for most real photos. **Fix (quick):** raise the limit in `next.config.ts`: ```ts const nextConfig: NextConfig = { experimental: { serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "8mb" } }, }; ``` **Fix (better, do eventually):** upload both blobs **client-side** directly to Supabase Storage (`supabase.storage.from("wardrobe").upload(...)` with the browser client — the storage RLS policy already scopes writes to `auth.uid()`), then pass only the two paths to the action. Kills the base64 inflation, the body limit, and bug #4's server-side blind spot in one move. --- ### 3. Module-scope `new Anthropic()` crashes the whole upload module without an API key **Where:** `lib/ai/tag-item.ts:7` **Bug:** `const client = new Anthropic()` runs at module init. With `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` blank (its current state in `.env.local`), importing `app/closet/upload/actions.ts` throws `Could not resolve apiKey` — so **both** actions 500, including `confirmItem`, which needs no AI at all. Even saving an already-tagged draft is impossible. **Fix:** construct lazily inside `tagItem`: ```ts let client: Anthropic | null = null; export async function tagItem(...) { client ??= new Anthropic(); // fails only here, only when tagging ... } ``` --- ### 4. Storage upload errors are silently swallowed → items with permanently missing images **Where:** `app/closet/upload/actions.ts:27-32` **Bug:** `supabase.storage.upload()` **returns** `{ error }` — it does not throw. Both calls discard the result. If either upload fails (RLS rejection, missing bucket, transient network/5xx), the action still tags and returns paths; the user confirms; `confirmItem` inserts an items row pointing at objects that don't exist. The photo is lost forever — the closet renders a blank card with no recovery except delete + re-capture. **Fix:** ```ts const { error: origErr } = await supabase.storage .from("wardrobe").upload(`${base}/original.jpg`, orig, { contentType: "image/jpeg" }); if (origErr) throw new Error(`Upload failed: ${origErr.message}`); const { error: cutErr } = await supabase.storage .from("wardrobe").upload(`${base}/cutout.png`, cut, { contentType: "image/png" }); if (cutErr) throw new Error(`Upload failed: ${cutErr.message}`); ``` --- ## 🟠 High — broken user-facing flows ### 5. Two of four bottom-nav tabs 404 **Where:** `components/shell/mobile-nav.tsx:12-13` **Bug:** nav links to `/generate` (Stylist) and `/calendar` (Diary), but neither route exists (`app/` only has `auth`, `closet`, `onboarding`, `profile`). Tapping either lands on Next's 404 page, which has no MobileNav — only browser-back recovers. **Fix (until plans 06/09 land):** add stub routes with a "coming soon" screen inside the mobile shell (mirroring the old closet stub), **or** render those tabs disabled/ghosted. Delete the stubs when plan 06 (generator) and plan 09 (calendar) are built. ### 6. Auth failure is silently invisible **Where:** `app/auth/callback/route.ts:24` + `app/page.tsx` **Bug:** on `exchangeCodeForSession` failure the callback redirects to `/?error=auth`, but `app/page.tsx` never reads `searchParams` — the user lands on the welcome screen with zero feedback. Classic trigger: opening the magic link in a different browser than the one that requested it (PKCE verifier cookie missing) or an expired link. Retrying loops silently. **Fix:** read the param in the Welcome page and render a notice: ```tsx export default async function Welcome({ searchParams, }: { searchParams: Promise<{ error?: string }> }) { const { error } = await searchParams; ... {error === "auth" && (

Sign-in link expired or was opened in a different browser. Please request a new one.

)} } ``` --- ## 🟡 Medium — data integrity & conventions ### 7. Item detail Save fabricates data on cleared fields **Where:** `components/closet/item-detail.tsx:61-63` **Bug:** empty material is silently written as `"Unknown"`; empty seasons becomes `["Spring"]` — so a user who deselects all seasons gets an item the generator will exclude 9 months a year, with no feedback. The capture confirm screen handles the same case differently (blocks deselecting the last season) — two screens disagree on one operation. **Fix:** reuse the capture flow's guard — in `toggleSeason`, refuse to remove the last selected season; require non-empty material before enabling Save (or keep the previous value instead of substituting "Unknown"). ### 8. `original.jpg` stores non-JPEG bytes with a JPEG content type **Where:** `app/closet/upload/actions.ts:27` + `lib/images/options.ts` **Bug:** `browser-image-compression` preserves the input MIME type (no `fileType` set), so a PNG/WebP library photo is uploaded as PNG/WebP bytes under `original.jpg` with `contentType: "image/jpeg"`. Permanent mislabel (originals are captured once); bites any consumer that trusts the declared type (Phase-2 share cards, exports, re-tagging). **Fix:** force JPEG in `lib/images/options.ts`: ```ts export function compressionOptions() { return { maxSizeMB: 0.5, maxWidthOrHeight: 1280, useWebWorker: true, fileType: "image/jpeg" }; } ``` ### 9. CLAUDE.md violation: colors / pattern / subcategory are not user-editable **Where:** `app/closet/[itemId]/actions.ts:9` (UpdateSchema) + both edit screens **Bug:** CLAUDE.md mandates *"Tags are always user-editable — treat AI tags as a draft."* When Haiku mis-tags colors or pattern (the ~10 % case the confirm screen exists for), the user cannot fix them anywhere — and wrong colors will directly poison the plan-06 color- harmony scoring. **Fix:** add `colors`, `pattern`, `subcategory` to `UpdateSchema` and expose editors — colors as chip multi-select (curated palette), pattern as the 5-value chip row — on both the capture confirm screen and item detail. ### 10. CLAUDE.md violation: no RLS tenant tests **Where:** `supabase/migrations/20260615114702_items.sql:23` **Bug:** CLAUDE.md conventions: *"RLS: every table … Add tenant tests."* The items table + wardrobe storage policies shipped with a full Vitest harness in the same diff but zero tests asserting user A cannot read user B's items/objects. A future policy edit that opens cross-tenant reads ships silently. **Fix:** add an integration test against local Supabase: create two users, insert an item as A, assert B's client gets zero rows from `items` and a 403/empty from signing A's storage path. (Plan 00's testing approach already calls for exactly this.) ### 11. Apple OAuth `env()` references may break `supabase start` (plausible, env-dependent) **Where:** `supabase/config.toml:276-278` **Bug:** the **disabled** Apple block uses `env(SUPABASE_AUTH_EXTERNAL_APPLE_CLIENT_ID)` / `env(...APPLE_SECRET)`. Some Supabase CLI versions error on unset env() references at config parse even when `enabled = false`. A contributor sourcing only the documented Google vars may fail `supabase start`. **Fix:** while disabled, use literal empty strings (`client_id = ""`, `secret = ""`) and restore the `env()` form when Apple ships — or add both vars (blank) to `.env.local` + LOCAL_DEV.md. Verify with a clean-env `supabase start` first; skip if your CLI version tolerates it. --- ## 🟢 Lower priority — hygiene, efficiency, dead code ### 12. Orphaned storage objects on abandoned captures **Where:** `app/closet/upload/actions.ts:22` Images are uploaded **before** confirm with no cleanup path. Every abandoned capture or tagging failure leaks two objects, forever — unbounded storage growth and invisible data for the GDPR deletion pipeline. **Fix:** upload at confirm time (natural if you take bug #2's "better" fix), or write drafts under a `drafts/` prefix that a scheduled cleanup expires. ### 13. Serial awaits on the magic-moment path **Where:** `app/closet/upload/actions.ts:27-34` The two uploads and the tagging call are mutually independent (`tagItem` uses `cutoutB64` from memory) but run sequentially — several avoidable seconds on the spinner. **Fix:** `await Promise.all([uploadOriginal, uploadCutout, tagItem(...)])` (checking each result per bug #4). Same pattern in `app/closet/[itemId]/page.tsx:28` — the brands query can run in `Promise.all` with the item fetch. ### 14. Domain vocabulary triplicated **Where:** `components/capture/capture-flow.tsx:11-17`, `components/closet/item-detail.tsx:10-16`, `components/closet/closet-grid.tsx:8` `CATEGORIES` / `SEASONS` / `FORMALITY_LABEL` / 14-entry `MATERIALS` are copy-pasted across three files and will drift. **Fix:** derive categories/seasons from `TagSchema` enums (`TagSchema.shape.category.options`) in one shared module, e.g. `lib/closet/vocab.ts`. ### 15. Dead filter logic **Where:** `lib/closet/filter.ts:13` `filterItems` re-checks `archived` client-side though every caller already queries `.eq("archived", false)`, and the `color` filter param has no consumer. **Fix:** reduce it to the category match it actually performs (and its tests along with it). ### 16. Unused motion variants lock in a dead dependency **Where:** `lib/motion.ts:4` `fcRise` / `fcFade` / `fcPop` have zero runtime consumers — only the test imports them, so the suite green-lights an export surface that can silently rot. **Fix:** wire the variants into the shipped screens (capture confirm, closet grid entrances — plan 03 intended this) or drop the module + test until a consumer lands. --- ## Suggested fix order 1. **#1 + #3** (`tag-item.ts` / `tagging-schema.ts`) — one edit session, makes tagging callable 2. **#4** (upload error checks) — 5 lines 3. **#2** (body size limit — quick fix now, client-side upload later) 4. → **e2e-test capture with the API key** (the original next step in STATE.md) 5. **#5, #6, #7** — user-facing polish, each small 6. **#9, #10** — CLAUDE.md compliance (colors editable, tenant tests) 7. **#8, #11–#16** — opportunistic, or fold into plan-06 prep *Not bugs, but open scope from STATE.md: onboarding 5-item capture (plan 04 task 9) not built; `/onboarding` doesn't redirect already-onboarded users away; plan 06 (generator) not started.*

content.content:
1	# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why
2	
3	_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._
4	
5	The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
6	(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):
7	
8	> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*
9	
10	> ⚠️ **The price is €5/mo, not £5** (decided 2026-08-05). The quote above is the design verbatim and is
11	> left intact as the citation it is, but **£ was a design-file artefact**: the app targets the EU, Supabase
12	> is EU-region, and every price already renders in euro (`lib/closet/wear-stats.ts` uses `en-IE` /
13	> `currency: "EUR"`). A Pro card reading £5 on a screen where cost-per-wear reads €3.00 is a visible
14	> inconsistency. **`2026-07-24-profile-hub.md` instructs "render that copy verbatim" — that instruction is
15	> superseded for the price only;** the feature list still ships verbatim.
16	
17	Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
18	**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
19	paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds
24	
25	Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.
26	
27	- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
28	- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
29	  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
30	  it in month three, once the data is theirs.
31	
32	Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:
33	
34	| Never gate | Why |
35	|---|---|
36	| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
37	| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
38	| **Tagging, item editing, and the closet's *quality*** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. **Amended 2026-08-05:** a generous SIZE cap (50, see §2) is now in place, but nothing about how a closet works is gated — no reduced tagging, no locked fields, no degraded stylist. The cap is a ceiling on quantity, never on capability. |
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 2. The meter: three rerolls a day
43	
44	> **AMENDED 2026-08-04.** This section previously read *"Free gets 3 AI generations per day"*, counting
45	> the daily drop toward that three. **It contradicted §1 of this same document**, which says the daily
46	> drop must never be gated — with drops counted, a free user who has viewed three occasions is refused
47	> the fourth, which is precisely gating the drop. §1 is what matches Decision 4 in `CLAUDE.md`, so §2 is
48	> the part that gave. The old wording is also what `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` disagreed with; all
49	> three documents now say the same thing.
50	
51	**Every occasion's first look of the day is free, on every tier. Free gets three rerolls a day, pooled
52	across all occasions. Pro rerolls without limit.**
53	
54	> **Pooled, not per-occasion** (decided 2026-08-05). A per-occasion allowance was built first and
55	> reverted: most people care about ONE occasion on a given day, so rationing per occasion is strictest
56	> exactly where attention goes and generous where nobody is looking — you could be refused a second Work
57	> reroll while holding an unused Evening one you never wanted. The usual objection to a shared pool, that
58	> it can block an occasion you have not opened, **does not apply once drops are free**: tapping a new
59	> occasion is always a drop, so the pool only ever meters rerolls.
60	
61	A "generation" is any call that spends a model request. There are three kinds, and they are metered
62	differently:
63	
64	| Kind | Free | Pro |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| **`drop`** — an occasion's first look of the day | Always free | Always free |
67	| **`regenerate`** — asking an occasion again | 3 per day, all occasions | Unlimited |
68	| **`styled`** — building a look around a chosen piece | Gated (Pro #2) | Unlimited |
69	
70	Reading a look that already exists is always free and always unlimited, per Decision 5 — including
71	re-opening a styled look, which is cached per (user, item, local day).
72	
73	The limit bites at the honest moment: someone rerolling a third time is genuinely dissatisfied, which is
74	when "Pro rerolls without limit" is a fair offer rather than a toll.
75	
76	**No counter is displayed** (decided 2026-08-05). The user is not told how many rerolls remain before
77	they run out. A visible "1 left" badge makes every free user think about the limit constantly, which is
78	the opposite of this section's design — *a user who never thinks about the limit never hits it*.
79	
80	### The ceiling, which is the number that matters
81	
82	Four occasion drops plus three rerolls:
83	
84	```
85	7 × $0.003 = $0.021/day  →  $0.63/user/month absolute worst case
86	```
87	
88	Realistic use is 2–3 generations a day, so ≈ $0.20/month. **The ceiling is the point:** a free tier needs
89	a worst case you can survive, and it must not scale with closet size. This is why `styled` is Pro rather
90	than "first time per item free" — the latter has no ceiling at all, since a 150-item closet would permit
91	150 free generations a day, and it would leave nothing in Pro #2 to sell.
92	
93	### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe
94	
95	Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:
96	
97	```
98	(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
99	```
100	
101	| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
102	|---|---|
103	| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
104	| Free user maxing the ceiling — 7/day | **≈ $0.63** |
105	| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs €5 revenue) |
106	
107	Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever.
108	
109	### Closet size: 50 pieces free (decided 2026-08-05)
110	
111	**A free closet holds 50 pieces. Pro is unlimited.**
112	
113	A 10-per-day rate limit was built first and removed in favour of this: with a ceiling in place the rate
114	was redundant, and two overlapping rules made the free tier feel meaner than it is — a new user would
115	have needed five days to reach 50, throttled during exactly the days you want them filling their closet.
116	One rule is easier to explain and easier to sell against.
117	
118	**The cap counts UNARCHIVED pieces.** Nothing in the product deletes an item, so counting archived ones
119	would strand a user at the cap with no way back under it. Archiving is the intended way to make room,
120	and an archived piece is not in your closet by any reading of the word.
121	
122	This section previously read *"Do not cap closet size"* full stop. What survives of that reasoning, and
123	why **50** rather than a tighter number:

# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why

_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._

The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):

> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*

> ⚠️ **The price is €5/mo, not £5** (decided 2026-08-05). The quote above is the design verbatim and is
> left intact as the citation it is, but **£ was a design-file artefact**: the app targets the EU, Supabase
> is EU-region, and every price already renders in euro (`lib/closet/wear-stats.ts` uses `en-IE` /
> `currency: "EUR"`). A Pro card reading £5 on a screen where cost-per-wear reads €3.00 is a visible
> inconsistency. **`2026-07-24-profile-hub.md` instructs "render that copy verbatim" — that instruction is
> superseded for the price only;** the feature list still ships verbatim.

Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.

---

## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds

Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.

- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
  it in month three, once the data is theirs.

Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:

| Never gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
| **Tagging, item editing, and the closet's *quality*** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. **Amended 2026-08-05:** a generous SIZE cap (50, see §2) is now in place, but nothing about how a closet works is gated — no reduced tagging, no locked fields, no degraded stylist. The cap is a ceiling on quantity, never on capability. |

---

## 2. The meter: three rerolls a day

> **AMENDED 2026-08-04.** This section previously read *"Free gets 3 AI generations per day"*, counting
> the daily drop toward that three. **It contradicted §1 of this same document**, which says the daily
> drop must never be gated — with drops counted, a free user who has viewed three occasions is refused
> the fourth, which is precisely gating the drop. §1 is what matches Decision 4 in `CLAUDE.md`, so §2 is
> the part that gave. The old wording is also what `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` disagreed with; all
> three documents now say the same thing.

**Every occasion's first look of the day is free, on every tier. Free gets three rerolls a day, pooled
across all occasions. Pro rerolls without limit.**

> **Pooled, not per-occasion** (decided 2026-08-05). A per-occasion allowance was built first and
> reverted: most people care about ONE occasion on a given day, so rationing per occasion is strictest
> exactly where attention goes and generous where nobody is looking — you could be refused a second Work
> reroll while holding an unused Evening one you never wanted. The usual objection to a shared pool, that
> it can block an occasion you have not opened, **does not apply once drops are free**: tapping a new
> occasion is always a drop, so the pool only ever meters rerolls.

A "generation" is any call that spends a model request. There are three kinds, and they are metered
differently:

| Kind | Free | Pro |
|---|---|---|
| **`drop`** — an occasion's first look of the day | Always free | Always free |
| **`regenerate`** — asking an occasion again | 3 per day, all occasions | Unlimited |
| **`styled`** — building a look around a chosen piece | Gated (Pro #2) | Unlimited |

Reading a look that already exists is always free and always unlimited, per Decision 5 — including
re-opening a styled look, which is cached per (user, item, local day).

The limit bites at the honest moment: someone rerolling a third time is genuinely dissatisfied, which is
when "Pro rerolls without limit" is a fair offer rather than a toll.

**No counter is displayed** (decided 2026-08-05). The user is not told how many rerolls remain before
they run out. A visible "1 left" badge makes every free user think about the limit constantly, which is
the opposite of this section's design — *a user who never thinks about the limit never hits it*.

### The ceiling, which is the number that matters

Four occasion drops plus three rerolls:

```
7 × $0.003 = $0.021/day  →  $0.63/user/month absolute worst case
```

Realistic use is 2–3 generations a day, so ≈ $0.20/month. **The ceiling is the point:** a free tier needs
a worst case you can survive, and it must not scale with closet size. This is why `styled` is Pro rather
than "first time per item free" — the latter has no ceiling at all, since a 150-item closet would permit
150 free generations a day, and it would leave nothing in Pro #2 to sell.

### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe

Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:

```
(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
```

| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
|---|---|
| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
| Free user maxing the ceiling — 7/day | **≈ $0.63** |
| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs €5 revenue) |

Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever.

was redundant, and two overlapping rules made the free tier feel meaner than it is — a new user would
have needed five days to reach 50, throttled during exactly the days you want them filling their closet.

1	# Settings Implementation Plan
2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
4	
5	**Goal:** Build `/settings` — the account row, the preference toggles, language, location, and sign-out — with every toggle actually persisted and actually read by the code it claims to control.
6	
7	**Architecture:** One `preferences jsonb` column on `profiles` rather than a column per toggle, so adding the fifth preference is not a migration. A Server Action writes a partial patch; a typed reader with defaults means a profile written before a toggle existed still behaves correctly.
8	
9	**Tech Stack:** Next.js 16 App Router, Supabase, Zod 4, Vitest.
10	
11	## Global Constraints
12	
13	- **TDD, strictly.** Branch: `feat/settings`. No AI attribution.
14	- **A toggle that nothing reads is a lie.** Every switch shipped here must change real behaviour in this same PR, or must not ship. Task 4 is where that is enforced.
15	- **No billing.** The Pro row renders inert; subscription is a later phase.
16	- **Depends on `2026-07-24-profile-hub.md`** only for the route to be reachable from the hub. It can be built in parallel and linked afterwards.
17	- Test: `npx vitest run <path>` / `npm run test:run`. Types: `npx tsc --noEmit`. Build: `npm run build`.
18	
19	## Source
20	
21	`design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821`. Review: `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` §6.7.
22	
23	The design's four toggles (`docs/prototype-review.md` §12): **Daily fit reminder · Rain guard · Auto-log
24	worn looks · Metric units & °C**.
25	
26	## Scope decisions
27	
28	| Toggle | Decision |
29	|---|---|
30	| **Rain guard** ("never suede in rain") | **Ship it.** `weatherRules` already excludes suede and canvas when it rains — this switch turns that off, which is a two-line change and the only toggle whose behaviour already exists. |
31	| **Auto-log worn looks** | **Ship it.** Read by the daily-drop path: when on, opening a look after 18:00 local logs it. Needs the wear-logging plan. |
32	| **Daily fit reminder** | **Do not ship.** It needs web-push, which CLAUDE.md defers to Phase 2. Rendering a switch that schedules nothing is the lie this plan is trying to avoid. |
33	| **Metric units & °C** | **Do not ship as a toggle.** Open-Meteo is requested in °C and every surface assumes it. Show the current unit as a read-only row until an imperial path exists. |
34	| **Language EN · DE** | **Render, disabled.** next-intl is deferred; the control shows EN selected with DE marked "Soon". |
35	
36	That leaves **two live toggles**. Fewer switches that work beats four that mostly do not.
37	
38	## File structure
39	
40	| File | Responsibility | Change |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| `supabase/migrations/20260724110000_profile_preferences.sql` | `profiles.preferences jsonb` | **Create** |
43	| `lib/profile/preferences.ts` | Schema, defaults, typed reader | **Create** |
44	| `lib/profile/__tests__/preferences.test.ts` | Its tests | **Create** |
45	| `app/settings/actions.ts` | `updatePreferences` | **Create** |
46	| `app/settings/page.tsx` | The route | **Create** |
47	| `components/settings/settings-view.tsx` | The screen | **Create** |
48	| `lib/generator/rules.ts` | `weatherRules` honours rain guard | Modify |
49

52	### Task 1: The preferences column

60	-- migration per toggle is friction that leads to toggles living in localStorage
61	-- instead. Defaults live in lib/profile/preferences.ts, not here, so a profile
62	-- row written before a preference existed still reads correctly.

72	### Task 2: Typed preferences
73	
74	**Files:** Create `lib/profile/preferences.ts` + test

80	```ts
81	import { readPreferences, PreferencesSchema } from "../preferences";
82	
83	test("an empty profile gets safe defaults", () => {
84	  const p = readPreferences({});
85	  expect(p.rainGuard).toBe(true);   // protective behaviour is the default
86	  expect(p.autoLogWorn).toBe(false); // writing data on the user's behalf is not
87	});
88	
89	test("a stored value overrides its default", () => {
90	  expect(readPreferences({ rainGuard: false }).rainGuard).toBe(false);
91	});
92

94	  expect(readPreferences(null).rainGuard).toBe(true);

96	  expect(readPreferences({ rainGuard: "yes" }).rainGuard).toBe(true);
97	});

100	  expect(readPreferences({ rainGuard: true, futureThing: 1 })).not.toHaveProperty("futureThing");
101	});

112	```ts
113	import { z } from "zod";
114	
115	/**
116	 * Defaults live here, not in the database, so a row written before a preference
117	 * existed reads correctly instead of behaving as `undefined`.
118	 *
119	 * `rainGuard` defaults ON because the protective behaviour already shipped and
120	 * silently changing it would be a regression. `autoLogWorn` defaults OFF
121	 * because it writes history on the user's behalf, and opting someone into
122	 * data-writing without asking is not ours to do.
123	 */
124	export const PreferencesSchema = z.object({
125	  rainGuard: z.boolean().default(true),
126	  autoLogWorn: z.boolean().default(false),
127	});
128	export type Preferences = z.infer<typeof PreferencesSchema>;
129	
130	export function readPreferences(raw: unknown): Preferences {
131	  const parsed = PreferencesSchema.safeParse(raw ?? {});
132	  return parsed.success ? parsed.data : PreferencesSchema.parse({});
133	}
134	```

145	- [ ] **Step 1: Implement**
146	
147	```ts
148	"use server";
149	
150	import { revalidatePath } from "next/cache";
151	import { createClient } from "@/lib/supabase/server";
152	import { PreferencesSchema, readPreferences } from "@/lib/profile/preferences";
153	
154	/**
155	 * Merge-patch, not replace: two settings screens open at once must not have the
156	 * last save silently revert the other's toggle.
157	 */
158	export async function updatePreferences(patch: unknown): Promise<void> {
159	  const data = PreferencesSchema.partial().parse(patch);
160	  const supabase = await createClient();
161	  const {
162	    data: { user },
163	  } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
164	  if (!user) throw new Error("Not signed in");
165	
166	  const { data: row } = await supabase
167	    .from("profiles")
168	    .select("preferences")
169	    .eq("id", user.id)
170	    .single();
171	
172	  const next = { ...readPreferences(row?.preferences), ...data };
173	  const { error } = await supabase.from("profiles").update({ preferences: next }).eq("id", user.id);
174	  if (error) throw new Error(error.message);
175	
176	  revalidatePath("/settings");
177	  revalidatePath("/generate");
178	}
179	```

content.text:
Read all four. Here's where things stand and what I'd want decided before writing any code.

## State (verified against git, not the docs)

`main` = `6de4730`, tree clean, no open PRs, nothing in flight. STATE.md's narrative matches git — it's current.

Queue #1–#9a are all merged (PRs #16, #18, #19, #20, #22, #23, #25, #27). **Next is #9b `settings`.**

`BUGS.md` is the 2026-07-04 review and is almost entirely historical — #1–#4 (tagging schema, body limit, lazy Anthropic client, swallowed upload errors), #5 (404 nav tabs), #9 (editable tags) and #14 (triplicated vocab) have all shipped since. I'd treat it as an archive, not a worklist.

## The settings plan is stale in five places

I read it against the code. It cannot be executed as written:

1. **Task 4 Step 4 — auto-log.** Already rejected (README, agreed with you 2026-08-05): opening a look isn't wearing it, and `wear_logs` is what all of Pro's analytics is built on. Must be cut, and `autoLogWorn` comes out of `PreferencesSchema` and its tests along with it.
2. **Task 5 Step 3 says "inert Pro banner (£5/mo)."** Price is €5, and PR #27 shipped `components/billing/pro-card.tsx` + the shared `UpgradeSheet`. Settings should reuse them or drop the banner — a second hand-rolled inert banner is exactly the divergence the shared sheet exists to prevent.
3. **Task 4's rain-guard signature.** `lib/generator/rules.ts:104` is still `weatherRules(w: Weather)` — one arg. The plan's three tests are correct as written, and the heat list is present, so its third test stays.
4. **Sign-out.** `app/profile/page.tsx:71` holds it with a comment saying the design moves it to Settings. That move is real work in this plan, not a note.
5. **Toggle count.** With auto-log gone, Settings ships **one** live toggle: rain guard.

## Two decisions I want from you before coding

**1. Is one live toggle enough to be a screen?** With auto-log removed, `/settings` is: account row, one working switch, a disabled DE control, a read-only location row, a read-only °C row, a Pro card, and sign-out. That's a real screen (sign-out has to live somewhere, and the `preferences` jsonb column is the seam every future toggle needs), but it's thinner than the plan assumed. The alternative is to skip ahead and take **#11 `styled-look-depth` Task 1** first — the README calls it independent and "a cheap real quality win": the styled shortlist skips `diversify`, so the model picks between 20 variations of one idea. That's a visible quality bug in a Pro feature. Settings is plumbing; #11 Task 1 makes the product better. I'd do #11 Task 1 first, then Settings.

**2. The evening wear-confirmation — its own plan now, or later?** You and I agreed it replaces auto-log: after ~18:00, if you opened a look and logged nothing, ask once, *Yes / No*, equally weighted. It's genuinely the better feature and it feeds the data Pro sells. But it's a new surface with real design questions (where does the prompt live — a sheet? the diary?), so it wants a brainstorm, not a task bolted onto Settings. My call: write it as a separate small plan, but not this session unless you want it.

Tell me which and I'll start. If you'd rather I just execute #9b as-is with the five corrections above folded in, say so and I'll branch.

content.text:
Confirmed 1, 2, 4. Point 3 explained, and one real problem with 5.

## Point 3, plainly

That one wasn't a staleness item — it was me checking the plan's starting assumption still holds. Task 4 says "give `weatherRules` a second argument so it can be told whether rain guard is on." I looked: `lib/generator/rules.ts:104` is still `weatherRules(w: Weather)`, one argument. So the plan's three tests are correct as written and nothing needs changing. Nothing for you to decide — I should have just said "checked, still fine."

## Point 5 — two of your three are cheap, one is not

**Rain guard** — settled, ships.

**Metric units °C/°F** — the plan said don't ship it. **The plan is wrong and I'll build it.** I traced every temperature in the codebase: the generator's thresholds are Celsius physics (`HOT_C = 25`, outerwear below 15°) and must stay Celsius, but the display sites are only five — `weather-strip.tsx` ×3, `advice.ts`, and `outfits/[id]/page.tsx`. So it's a `formatTemp(tempC, unit)` helper at the render boundary plus threading one preference. An hour of work, fully honest. The model prompt in `rerank.ts` stays °C deliberately — that's internal, not something you read.

**Daily fit reminder** — this one I can't build honestly right now, and here's the concrete reason rather than the plan's hand-wave. There is **no service worker in the project at all**: `public/` has none, the manifest has no push config, no VAPID keys, no subscription table, no scheduler. A daily reminder at 8am local needs all five of those plus a cron that knows each user's timezone. And a caveat specific to us: **iOS delivers web push only to PWAs actually installed to the home screen** — for anyone using Fitcheck in a Safari tab, the switch would be on and silently do nothing, which is the exact failure the plan's own rule is about.

**My recommendation: it goes in the wear-confirmation plan, not Settings.** You've already put that plan immediately after this one, and it's the same feature — the evening confirmation is "nudge the user at a time of day," the fit reminder is "nudge the user at a time of day." One notification mechanism, built once, serving both. Building push inside Settings means building it twice.

That gives Settings **two live toggles that both work** (rain guard, units), and the reminder ships a plan later with the machinery it actually needs.

If you'd rather I build web-push now and have Settings carry all three, say so and I'll do it — but it's a multi-day piece pulled out of Phase 2, and it makes Settings a notifications project.

## Ordering — does it matter?

You asked what the difference is. Technically: **almost none.** They share no files — Settings touches `profiles.preferences`, `app/settings/`, `lib/profile/`, and one signature in `rules.ts`; look-depth Task 1 touches only `style-actions.ts` to add the missing `diversify` call. No dependency in either direction.

But there's one asymmetry that decides it: **the wear-confirmation plan you want next needs `profiles.preferences` to exist** — at minimum for "don't ask again today," probably for an opt-out too. Settings creates that column. So Settings first puts the thing you asked for next directly behind its prerequisite, and look-depth Task 1 is small enough that waiting costs it nothing.

**Settings → look-depth → wear-confirmation**, unless you want the quick win merged first.

Give me the nod on the reminder and I'll branch `feat/settings` and start.

**The wear-confirmation feature needs no notification system at all.** It triggers when the app is next opened after ~18:00 local — it's an in-app prompt, zero push, buildable today. I lumped it together with the reminder last message; that was sloppy.

So it's only the **daily fit reminder** that needs the push stack, and it's the only thing in the product that does. /**
 * Fabrics that are wrong in real heat NO MATTER HOW THEY ARE MADE.
 *
 * This is the measured replacement for the season tag's incidental thermal
 * protection: season used to be a hard filter, so a sweater tagged
 * {Autumn,Winter} could never reach a July outfit. Season is now a preference
 * (see ./season.ts), so the guard moved to the temperature we already fetch.
 *
 * The list is deliberately SHORT, and notably does not contain wool.
 * Whether a wool garment suits 30°C is decided by its weight and weave, not its
 * fibre: tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting, and merino is
 * used *for* heat because it wicks and breathes. `items.material` is a bare
 * fibre name today, so a "wool" rule cannot tell a summer-weight trouser from a
 * melton coat — it would exclude exactly the smart-casual work wear this app is
 * built around. Everything left here is insulation or a coarse heavy weave,
 * where no construction makes it summer-appropriate.
 *
 * Wool, merino and cashmere are not unprotected: an off-season piece still takes
 * the `seasonFit` penalty in scoring, so it ranks below linen in July. Demoted
 * on evidence rather than eliminated on a guess — the same argument this module
 * makes about season itself.
 *
 * The real fix is data, not a longer list. `item-data-completeness` (queue #3)
 * adds an `items.texture` column — Flat / Fine knit / Chunky knit / Brushed /
 * Fleece-back — and constrains `material` to a vocabulary that separates "Wool"
 * from "Merino wool". `item-signals-in-generator` (queue #12) then feeds
 * material × texture into SCORING. Warmth belongs there, as a weighted signal,
 * not here as a veto.
 */
const HOT_MATERIALS = ["fleece", "shearling", "down", "quilted", "puffer", "tweed"];

/** Strictly above 25: 24° is pleasant, 26° is hot. */
const HOT_C = 25;

export function weatherRules(w: Weather) {
  return {
    needsOuterwear: w.tempC < 15,
    excludeMaterials: [
      ...(w.rain ? ["suede", "canvas"] : []),
      ...(w.tempC > HOT_C ? HOT_MATERIALS : []),
    ],
  };
}

Confirmed **pre-existing on `main`** and unrelated to my change: with 1 top / 1 bottom / 2 shoes the walk emits the same combo twice and `s2` is unreachable.

Root cause is the shoe stride at `candidates.ts:176` — `shoes[(t + d * 2) % shoes.length]`. When there's one top, `t` is always 0, so the index is `2d % shoes.length`, which is permanently 0 whenever `shoes.length` is 2. PR #14 measured shoe coverage on a 20-top closet, where `t` supplied the variation and masked it.

STATE.md's convention is that incidental fixes ride along with the branch in flight, so I'm fixing it here in its own commit.

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
feat(settings): the settings screen

Account row, two working preference toggles, the language control, a
read-only location row and sign out. Sign out moves here from the profile
hub, which was holding it only until this route existed.

Two deliberate divergences from Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821. The Pro banner
(:794) is dropped: the profile hub already owns the single Pro entry point
and opens the shared UpgradeSheet, and two cards on two screens can drift
into disagreeing about what Pro is. The account row's chevron (:791) is
dropped because it implies an account detail screen that does not exist --
two bottom-nav tabs used to 404 for that exact reason.

The design's four toggles become two, and both change real behaviour in
this same PR. The daily fit reminder is not among them: it needs web-push,
and no service worker, VAPID keys or scheduler exist, so it ships with the
notifications plan rather than as a switch that schedules nothing.

Toggles are optimistic and revert on a failed write with a visible message.
A switch that waits for a round trip reads as broken; one that stays moved
after a failed save is worse, because the screen then disagrees with the
database and only a refresh reveals it. Track and knob geometry are inline
styles -- arbitrary-value utilities have silently failed to resolve in this
project three times, and a switch whose track collapses is not a switch.
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -4

content.text:
Correct — it's inert. That matches the design (`Fitcheck.dc.html:815-818` is a display row with no handler), but you've caught a real dead end, and there's a second problem underneath it.

**The dead end:** location is genuinely changeable — the picker lives on the Stylist screen's weather pill (city search + "Use my location"). Settings shows the value with no affordance and no hint about where to change it, so the row invites exactly the question you just asked.

**The inconsistency:** it currently reads "Not set" because `profiles.location_label` is null, while the Stylist screen is happily showing a default city. Two screens describing the same thing differently.

Three ways to close it:

1. **Read-only + a hint** — keep the row, show the *effective* location (the fallback, not "Not set"), add a muted "Change on Stylist" line. Cheapest, honest, no duplicate UI. Doesn't let you act from here.
2. **Make the row navigate** to the Stylist screen where the picker is. One tap to the real control, but a Location row that jumps you to the outfits screen is a strange landing.
3. **Build the picker into Settings** — city search + "Use my location" here too. Most "correct" for a settings screen, but it duplicates a control that already exists and works, so two places then have to stay in sync.

**I'd take 1**, and only because 3 is worth doing properly later rather than half-doing now: the picker involves geolocation permission, the `location_source` precedence rule (a saved city must beat GPS), and the silent-refresh race that PR #21 fixed. Duplicating that logic is how it drifts. If location deserves a real home in Settings, it should move there wholesale and come *out* of the weather pill — that's its own small plan, not a bolt-on.

Which do you want? And I'll fix the "Not set" mismatch either way.

content.text:
Read the whole location path. It's the most carefully-guarded code in the app — PR #21 fixed three separate bugs in it — so here's what "properly" actually requires, including one constraint that shapes the design.

**The blocker nobody would guess: timezone.** `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and today that value comes from `fetchForecast` (`&timezone=auto`). So location is only written *after* a successful generate, as a side-effect in `applyResult` (`stylist.tsx:186`). Settings has no generate, so it can't reuse that path.

That matters because `location_timezone` is load-bearing: `localDateFor` and `predictDefaultOccasion` read it, and a null falls back to UTC — which is exactly the bug Decision 5 exists to prevent (a UTC key rolls the daily drop over mid-evening). So Settings cannot write a location without resolving its timezone.

**The fix is a dedicated `setLocation` server action** that fetches the forecast purely to read `timezone`, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no key, no AI, and it's already cached 30 minutes per rounded coordinate. This is genuinely better than today's design: persistence stops being a side-effect of generating and becomes explicit.

**The shape:**

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| `lib/weather/use-location-picker.ts` | The hook: city search, permission probe, `getCurrentPosition`, `locating` / `geoError` / `geoSupported`, and the three refs that guard the silent refresh |
| `components/weather/location-picker.tsx` | The shared menu UI, lifted out of `weather-strip.tsx` |
| `setLocation` (server action) | Resolve timezone → persist → `revalidatePath` both screens |

Sync then falls out of the database rather than being wired: Stylist reads stored location through `resolveLocation` on mount, and `location_source: 'city'` already suppresses the GPS refresh via `geoAllowedRef` — so a city chosen in Settings survives, with no new rule.

**Two things I want your call on before I write a line:**

1. **Own PR, or ride along with Settings?** I'd strongly do it as its own plan and PR. It refactors the exact code PR #21 hardened, and burying that under "feat: settings" makes the diff hard to review and the revert-unit wrong. Settings is finished and green *now*; this would hold it hostage for a day.

2. **Does the weather-pill picker stay?** If Settings gets a real picker, the Stylist pill can either remain as a contextual shortcut (two entry points, one shared component — normal, and the pill is where you *notice* the weather is wrong) or be removed so Settings is the only home. I'd keep both, since they'd share one implementation and can't drift.

My recommendation: **merge Settings with the location row read-only plus a "Change on Stylist" hint, then do location as the next plan straight after.** You get Settings today and the location work done properly tomorrow, instead of one large PR where the risky part is hidden inside the safe part.

Say the word and I'll either write that plan or fold it in.

# Cutout Backfill Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Re-encode the PNG cutouts already in Storage as WebP, so existing closets get the same ~75% size drop new uploads get.

**Architecture:** The WebP plan only affects new captures — every garment uploaded before it keeps its 540–714 KB PNG forever. A one-off Node script walks `items` rows whose `cutout_url` ends in `.png`, re-encodes with `sharp` (preserving alpha), uploads the WebP alongside, and updates the row. It is idempotent, resumable, and dry-run by default. The old PNG is left in place until the run is verified.

**Tech Stack:** `sharp` (dev-only), `@supabase/supabase-js` with the service role, `tsx`.

## Global Constraints

- **Requires `docs/superpowers/plans/done/2026-07-22-webp-cutouts.md`** — merged, so new uploads are already WebP. (Backfilling before that shipped would have meant running it twice.)
- `sharp` is a **devDependency and a script-only import**. It must never be imported from `app/` or `lib/` — client-side, zero-cost image work is Decision 2, and this script is maintenance tooling, not app code.
- The service-role key is used **only here**, in a script run by hand, never in app code (which relies exclusively on RLS). Read it from the environment; never commit it.
- **Non-destructive.** Write the `.webp`, update the row, leave the `.png`. Deleting originals is a separate, later decision once the run is proven.
- Idempotent: re-running must skip rows already migrated, so an interrupted run can simply be run again.

---

## File Structure

| File | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `lib/images/paths.ts` | **Create.** Pure: derive the WebP path from a cutout path, and recognise what still needs migrating. |
| `scripts/backfill-cutouts.ts` | **Create.** The one-off run: list → re-encode → upload → update. |
| `package.json` | **Modify.** `sharp` + `tsx` as devDependencies; a `backfill:cutouts` script. |

It is idempotent, resumable, and dry-run by default. The old PNG is left in place until the run is verified.

**Tech Stack:** `sharp` (dev-only), `@supabase/supabase-js` with the service role, `tsx`.

- **Requires `docs/superpowers/plans/done/2026-07-22-webp-cutouts.md`** — merged, so new uploads are already WebP. (Backfilling before that shipped would have meant running it twice.)

- The service-role key is used **only here**, in a script run by hand, never in app code (which relies exclusively on RLS). Read it from the environment; never commit it.
- **Non-destructive.** Write the `.webp`, update the row, leave the `.png`. Deleting originals is a separate, later decision once the run is proven.
- Idempotent: re-running must skip rows already migrated, so an interrupted run can simply be run again.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Stop uploading for two minutes — this is time-critical, and right now it's free to fix.**

## Root cause

`lib/ai/tagging-schema.ts:79`:
```ts
colors: z.array(z.string()).min(1).max(3),   // ← free text
material: z.enum(MATERIALS),                  // ← constrained
texture: z.enum(TEXTURES),                    // ← constrained
```

PR #19 converted `material` and `texture` to enums but **left `colors` as free strings**, while in the same PR adding a 21-colour `ColorPicker`. Its own architecture line claims the opposite: *"vocab.ts becomes the single source for … the colour palette; the two edit surfaces **and the AI schema** all read from it."* The AI schema doesn't. That's the bug — an oversight in #19, not a decision.

So Haiku returns whatever it likes ("khaki", "off-white", "light blue"), and the picker only offers 21 names.

## It's worse than one mismatch — there are **four** colour vocabularies

| Where | Count | Disagrees how |
|---|---|---|
| `TagSchema.colors` | ∞ | unconstrained |
| `vocab.ts COLORS` | 21 | what the user can pick |
| `color.ts NEUTRALS` | 13 | has `khaki`, `ecru`, `gray` — **not pickable**; missing `silver`, `gold`, `camel`, `denim` |
| `color.ts COLOR_FAMILIES` | ~45 | **23 names the picker can never produce** (sand, oatmeal, taupe, ivory, greige, cognac, terracotta, cobalt, midnight, sage, forest, moss, graphite, onyx, jet…) |

And `color.ts:20-23` documents *why* families were widened: *"Item colours come from Haiku as free-form common names … so matching a swatch id verbatim found almost nothing."* That was the right fix **before** a curated palette existed. Now it's papering over the unconstrained schema.

**Real consequences:** `colorHex("khaki")` returns `undefined`, so such an item shows no swatch and the user can't reselect it; and `colorHarmonyScore` treats `silver`/`gold`/`camel` as *accents* while treating unpickable `khaki`/`ecru` as neutrals.

**Your database is empty.** Fixing this now costs nothing. If you upload 30 items first, they get free-text colours and need a normalisation pass — exactly like `scripts/backfill-item-tags.ts` had to do for materials (15 of 29 rows).

## What I'd do — but it's your call, and one part is genuinely yours

1. Constrain `TagSchema.colors` to `z.enum` derived from `vocab.ts COLORS` — the same treatment material/texture got.
2. Derive `NEUTRALS` and `COLOR_FAMILIES` from that palette, with a test asserting every name in them is a real palette colour (the guard `HOT_MATERIALS` already has in `vocab.test.ts`).

**The part I won't decide alone:** which of the 21 count as *neutral*. You know menswear and I'd rather not encode folk rules — `camel` is currently an accent, which for a camel coat seems wrong to me, and `denim`, `silver`, `gold` are all arguable. Tell me your list and I'll pin it with tests.

Also worth your judgement: 21 colours may be too coarse to describe a wardrobe honestly. The alternative is keeping free text and dropping the picker to a *suggestion* list — but then the swatch problem stays. I'd constrain.

Say go and I'll fix it before you upload; say later and I'll write the backfill instead.
