content.text:
All green — 532 tests, tsc clean. Now your question, which is the right one to ask.

**The constraint didn't reduce what *you* can pick.** The picker has offered exactly these 21 since PR #19 — that hasn't changed. What shrank is what *Haiku* could invent, which was unlimited. Before, the AI wrote colours you could never select or see a swatch for; now both sides use one list.

**But your instinct is correct — 21 has real gaps.** The worst:

- **There is no red.** A red sweater gets forced into `rust` or `burgundy`. Both are wrong.
- No **orange**, **purple**, **teal**.
- No **khaki** (a light drab tan — genuinely different from `olive`, which is green), no **taupe**, no **sage**, no light **sky** blue.

The old free-text system hid this: Haiku just wrote "red" and it *looked* fine, while `colorHex("red")` returned undefined, no swatch rendered, and `isNeutral`/`inFamily` both missed it. So the palette was always this small — the gap was just invisible.

Now it's cheap to fix: one list, and tests pin the schema, the picker and the generator families together.

**I'd add 8, taking it to 29:**

| Colour | Neutral? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| red | accent | the outright hole |
| orange | accent | `rust` is a muted earth tone, not orange |
| purple | accent | unrepresented |
| teal | accent | unrepresented |
| khaki | **neutral** | drab tan; pairs like a neutral, distinct from olive |
| taupe | **neutral** | the grey-brown nothing currently covers |
| sage | accent | soft green, very common in knitwear |
| sky | accent | light blue; `blue` reads mid-tone |

**Also, the neutral call I made** (I said I wouldn't decide it alone, then you said go, so here it is explicitly): neutrals are **black, charcoal, grey, white, cream, stone, beige, camel, tan, brown, navy, denim**. Everything else is an accent. The reasoning is that `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish. That's why **camel** and **denim** are neutral. Say the word if you'd move any.

Want the 8 added before you upload? It's a two-minute change and the tests already guard it.

TagSchema.colors was z.array(z.string()) — the only field PR #19 left free

"off-white", which colorHex() could not render and the user could not
reselect, and lib/generator/color.ts had meanwhile widened its lean families
with ~23 free-form names to catch that output. Three vocabularies drifting,
plus an unconstrained fourth.

Now one list. COLOR_NAMES lives beside MATERIALS and TEXTURES and the schema
is z.enum over it; vocab.ts attaches hex and a neutral flag; NEUTRALS and

palette colour and that the picker and the schema hold the same list.

value, and the item edit sheet narrows legacy text[] rows at the boundary
rather than offering an unknown colour back for re-saving.

The palette went 21 -> 42, because 21 was not honest: it had no red at all,
so a red garment was forced into rust or burgundy. Free text hid that, since
"red" simply rendered no swatch and matched no family. Added the full earth

content.text:
**Done — upload away.** 532 tests, tsc, build and lint all green.

## Palette: 21 → 42

| Group | Colours |
|---|---|
| Achromatic | black, charcoal, grey, silver, white, ivory, cream |
| Earths | stone, sand, beige, taupe, khaki, camel, tan, **caramel**, **chocolate**, brown |
| Blues | navy, indigo, denim, blue, sky, teal |
| Greens | olive, sage, forest, green, mint |
| Reds/pinks | burgundy, maroon, **red**, rust, terracotta, coral, pink |
| Purples | purple, lavender, plum |
| Yellows/oranges | mustard, yellow, gold, orange |

I stopped short of near-duplicates (ivory/ecru/off-white, burgundy/wine, camel/biscuit) on purpose — when two names describe the same colour the model picks between them at random, and every downstream lookup gets less reliable, not more. Say the word if any specific one you actually own is missing and I'll add it.

## What else changed

- **`ColorPicker` is now typed to the palette**, so the editor can't reintroduce a stray value either — that was the other open door.
- **The item edit sheet drops unknown colours** from legacy `text[]` rows instead of offering them back for re-saving.
- **Neutral vs accent is now explicit.** Foundations count as neutral: navy, indigo, denim, olive, khaki, camel, tan, caramel, chocolate, brown, taupe and the achromatics. Everything else is an accent. This matters because `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation an accent punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish.
- **Two of my earlier calls changed** in the process, so you know: **olive is now neutral** (I'd had it as an accent, and with khaki neutral that was inconsistent), and `khaki` — which I used as the example of an *invalid* colour an hour ago — is now a real one.

## One thing to eyeball when you add your first item

The picker panel is `flex-wrap`, so 42 swatches roughly doubles its height. It should wrap fine at 390px, but I haven't seen it on device — the DB is empty, so the capture confirm screen is the first place it renders. **Tell me how it looks on your first upload** and I'll adjust the swatch size if it's cramped.

After that I still owe you: the Location row fix, live verification of both toggles, the rain-guard proof (needs one suede or canvas item), and then the location-picker plan.

input.new_string:
### ✅ LIVE-VERIFIED end to end (2026-08-06)

**Rain guard was proven against a real forecast**, not a fixture. Manila was live-rainy (`fetchForecast`
reported `condition: "Rain"`, `rainNow: true`, 26°C); one of the three leather sneakers was temporarily
set to `Canvas`, the location temporarily set to Manila, and today's drop deleted between runs:

| `rainGuard` | Shoes the generator chose |
|---|---|
| `true` | Leather · Leather · Leather — the canvas pair never appears |
| `false` | Leather · Leather · **Canvas** |

That exercises the whole chain: `profiles.preferences` → `readPreferences` → `candidateArgs.rainGuard`
→ `weatherRules` → `eligibleByCategory` → `outfit_items`. **Two real Haiku calls were spent.**

**Fahrenheit was verified on the same screen:** `feels 31°C` rendered as `feels 88°F` (31 × 9/5 + 32 =
87.8). The headline moved 26° → 81° only because the forecast ticked to 27°C between loads.

**The write path was already proven by the user's own taps** — `profiles.preferences` held a written
`{"tempUnit":"C","rainGuard":true}` rather than the `{}` default before any of this testing began.

⚠️ **Synthetic clicks into the Simulator fail on this machine** with System Events `-25204`
(accessibility permission), so toggle taps must be done by hand; DB state is the way to drive
verification instead.

**All test data was reverted**: shoe back to `Leather`, location columns back to null, preferences back
to `{"tempUnit":"C","rainGuard":true}`, and `outfits` / `outfit_items` / `generation_events` cleared so
the user's reroll allowance was not consumed. Verified by query afterwards.

### ⚠️ Arbitrary-value Tailwind failed a FOURTH time on this branch

`ml-[6px]`, `text-[9.5px]` and `align-[1px]` on the Language row's "Soon" badge all silently failed to
resolve — the badge sat flush against the label and read as `DeutschSOON`. Same failure as `size-[32px]`,
`text-[12px]/[1.3]` and `bottom-[6px]`. **It was caught only by screenshotting the simulator**; tests and
tsc were green throughout. The rule holds and is now cheap to state: a NEW arbitrary value carrying
geometry goes in an inline `style`.

### ⚠️ The colour vocabulary was unconstrained — fixed on this branch, and the palette tripled

`TagSchema.colors` was `z.array(z.string())`: the ONLY field PR #19 left free while adding a 21-swatch
picker in the same PR. Its own architecture note claimed *"vocab.ts becomes the single source … and the
AI schema reads from it"* — the AI schema did not. So Haiku emitted names like `light blue` that
`colorHex()` could not render and the user could not reselect, and `lib/generator/color.ts` had widened
its lean families with ~23 free-form names (sand, oatmeal, cognac, terracotta, onyx…) to compensate.
**Four colour vocabularies, none agreeing.**

Now one: `COLOR_NAMES` sits beside `MATERIALS`/`TEXTURES`, the schema is `z.enum` over it, `vocab.ts`
attaches hex + a `neutral` flag, and `NEUTRALS`/`COLOR_FAMILIES` are derived with tests pinning that
every name in them is a real palette colour. `ColorPicker` is typed to the palette; the item edit sheet
narrows legacy `text[]` rows at the boundary.

**The palette went 21 → 42** (user decision — *"we need a lot of colors mate"*). 21 was not honest: it had
**no red at all**, so a red garment was forced into `rust` or `burgundy`. Free text hid that, because
"red" simply rendered no swatch and matched no family. Near-duplicates (ivory/ecru/off-white) were
deliberately NOT added — when two names describe one colour the model picks between them at random and
every downstream lookup gets less reliable.

**Neutral vs accent is a product decision, now explicit.** It drives `colorHarmonyScore`, which gives one
accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and
punishes a restrained outfit, whereas the reverse only fails to punish. Neutral: the achromatics plus
`taupe, khaki, camel, tan, caramel, chocolate, brown, navy, indigo, denim, olive`. ⚠️ **`olive` was
flipped from accent to neutral** partway through, once `khaki` joined as a neutral and the pair became
inconsistent.

**One legacy row was normalised:** an Oxford shirt uploaded 21 minutes before the fix landed carried
`light blue`; set to `sky`. Every colour in the closet is now a palette colour. Uploads after the fix
(`sky`, `ivory`) confirm the constraint is live.

### Location in Settings — DECIDED, and it is its own PR

User chose a **real picker in Settings, kept alongside the Stylist's weather pill**, both driven by one
shared component. **Not built on this branch** — it refactors the code PR #21 hardened.

⚠️ **The constraint that shapes it: `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value comes
from `fetchForecast`** (`&timezone=auto`), so today location is only written as a side-effect of a
successful generate (`stylist.tsx:186`). Settings has no generate. `location_timezone` is load-bearing —
`localDateFor` and `predictDefaultOccasion` read it and a null falls back to UTC, the exact bug Decision 5
exists to prevent. **So Settings needs a `setLocation` action that fetches the forecast purely to resolve
the timezone**, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no key, no AI, already cached 30 min per rounded
coordinate. Planned shape: `lib/weather/use-location-picker.ts` (hook) +
`components/weather/location-picker.tsx` (shared UI) + that action. Sync then falls out of the database:
`resolveLocation` already surfaces stored provenance and `location_source: 'city'` already suppresses the
GPS refresh via `geoAllowedRef`.

Interim on this branch: the row shows the **effective** location via `resolveLocation` (it read
`location_label` directly and said "Not set" while the Stylist showed Berlin) plus a "Change it on the
Stylist screen" hint, so it is no longer a dead end.

### Queue #13 `cutout-backfill` now has nothing to convert

No linked remote Supabase project and no Vercel deployment exist, local storage is at 0 legacy files, and
every new upload is already WebP (`lib/images/encode.ts`). The 10 legacy `cutout.png` files
`MONETISATION.md` cites as "the far bigger lever" are gone with the volume. **Move it out of the
execution order and mark it "run only if `.png` cutouts ever appear"** — `encode.ts:48` can still emit PNG
on the fallback path, so the script is idle rather than dead.

### The impeccable hook flags this screen's font sizes — left unchanged, deliberately

14.5px / 13.5px / 12.5px / 12px are `Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821`'s own values. Small type was **deferred to
the end of the project by decision on 2026-07-24**, and queue #16 owns the whole-product type audit.

**Rain guard**, against a real forecast — Manila was genuinely raining (`fetchForecast` returned `condition: "Rain"`). Same closet, same weather, same day, only the toggle differing:

| `rainGuard` | Shoes chosen |

**All test data reverted** — shoe back to leather, location back to null, preferences restored, and `outfits`/`generation_events` cleared so your reroll allowance wasn't spent. Two Haiku calls total.

## Two things the screenshots caught that tests could not

1. **Arbitrary-value Tailwind failed a fourth time.** `ml-[6px]`, `text-[9.5px]`, `align-[1px]` all silently didn't resolve, rendering `DeutschSOON` as one word. Tests and tsc were green the whole time. Fixed with inline styles.
2. **Your `light blue` Oxford** — uploaded 21 minutes before the colour fix landed. Normalised to `sky`. Everything you uploaded after uses the new palette (`sky`, `ivory` are both new names), so the constraint is confirmed live.

## Scope note

Four of the seven commits weren't in the Settings plan: the colour vocabulary fix, the palette expansion, the shoe-coverage bug, and the location row. I'd have kept them separate, but you raised each mid-flight and this project's convention is that fixes ride along with the branch in flight. The colour work in particular *had* to happen before you uploaded, or it needed a backfill.

## Not done, by your decision

- **Location picker in Settings** — own PR. I've recorded the constraint that shapes it in STATE.md: `saveLocation` needs `location_timezone`, which today only exists as a by-product of generating, so Settings needs its own `setLocation` action.

gh pr create --title "feat: settings" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Builds `/settings`: account row, preferences, language, location, sign out. Sign out moves here from the profile hub, which was holding it only until this route existed.

## Toggles

Two ship, and **both change real behaviour in this same PR**.

- **Rain guard** turns off the suede/canvas exclusion in `weatherRules`. It reaches the wet-material list only — the heat exclusions are about comfort at 30°, `needsOuterwear` is about cold, and a switch labelled "never suede in the rain" has no business touching either.
- **Metric units** ships as a real toggle. The plan said not to ("every surface assumes °C"), but only five display sites exist, so `formatTemp` converts at the render boundary and Celsius stays the storage and reasoning unit everywhere — Open-Meteo is requested in it, `weatherRules` compares against it, and the re-rank prompt states it to the model. `laterAdvice` is the one exception and takes the unit as an argument, because it bakes a temperature into prose server-side; its 5° trigger stays Celsius, since the physics is not a preference.

**Auto-log worn looks is deliberately absent.** Opening a look is not wearing it, and `wear_logs` is the foundation of everything Pro sells. **Daily fit reminder is absent too**: it needs web-push, and no service worker, VAPID keys or scheduler exist — plus iOS only delivers push to home-screen-installed PWAs, so the switch would be on and silently do nothing in a Safari tab. It ships with the notifications plan.

Preferences live in one `jsonb` column with defaults in TypeScript, so adding the next one is not a migration. The read path is lenient per-field (one malformed value cannot discard the others); the write path is strict, so garbage is rejected rather than repaired on every later read. Writes are merge-patches, so two open tabs cannot revert each other. Toggles are optimistic and revert on failure with a visible message.

## Divergences from `Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821`

- **No Pro banner** (`:794`). The profile hub owns the single Pro entry point and opens the shared `UpgradeSheet`; two cards on two screens can drift into disagreeing about what Pro is.
- **No chevron on the account row** (`:791`) — it implies an account detail screen that does not exist. Two bottom-nav tabs used to 404 for that reason.
- **Location row** shows the *effective* location via `resolveLocation` and says where to change it. It read `location_label` directly and said "Not set" while the Stylist showed Berlin. A real picker here is its own PR.

## Also on this branch

**Colours were an unconstrained vocabulary.** `TagSchema.colors` was `z.array(z.string())` — the only field #19 left free while adding a 21-swatch picker in the same PR, though its own architecture note claimed the AI schema read from `vocab.ts`. Haiku emitted names like `light blue` that `colorHex()` could not render and the user could not reselect, and `color.ts` had widened its lean families with ~23 free-form names to compensate: four vocabularies, none agreeing. Now one — `COLOR_NAMES` beside `MATERIALS`/`TEXTURES`, schema as `z.enum`, families and neutrals derived, tests pinning that every name in them is a real palette colour, and `ColorPicker` typed to the palette.

**The palette went 21 → 42.** 21 had no red at all, so a red garment was forced into rust or burgundy; free text hid it because "red" simply rendered no swatch and matched no family. Near-duplicates were deliberately excluded — two names for one colour means the model picks at random.

**`neutral` is now explicit per colour**, because `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after: calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish. So navy, denim, camel, khaki, chocolate and the rest of the menswear foundations count as neutral.

**A pre-existing generator defect, present on `main`.** `candidates.ts` indexed shoes at `(t + d * 2) % shoes.length`. With one top, `t` is always 0, so the index reduced to `2d % shoes.length` and never left 0 whenever that length was even — a two-shoe closet could only ever wear the first pair, and the same combo was emitted twice. `decorrelatedStride` picks a stride coprime with the count, keeping shoes off lockstep with bottoms while still visiting all of them. PR #14 measured shoe coverage on a 20-top closet, where the top index supplied the variation and hid this.

## Verification

Rain guard was proven against a live forecast rather than a fixture — Manila was genuinely raining. Same closet, same weather, same day, only the toggle differing:

| `rainGuard` | Shoes chosen |
|---|---|
| `true` | Leather · Leather · Leather — the canvas pair never appears |
| `false` | Leather · Leather · **Canvas** |

Fahrenheit verified on the same screen (`feels 31°C` → `feels 88°F`). Screenshotted on an iPhone 17 simulator, which is also what caught `ml-[6px]` / `text-[9.5px]` silently failing to resolve on the "Soon" badge — tests and tsc were green throughout.

533 tests · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · lint unchanged from main's baseline.
EOF

https://github.com/1curafu/Fitcheck/pull/28 — 7 commits, 33 files, mergeable. I've got a monitor watching CI and will report when `verify` lands.

## The plan is written

`docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-08-06-location-in-settings.md`, queued as **9c**. Seven TDD tasks. The two parts worth knowing about before you read it:

**1. It's shaped by a constraint, not by preference.** `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value only exists as a by-product of `fetchForecast` during a generate. Settings has no generate, and a null timezone falls back to UTC — the exact failure Decision 5 exists to prevent. So Task 1 builds a `setLocation` action that fetches the forecast purely to resolve the timezone. Notably `saveLocation` must *not* also do that fetch: it runs inside `applyResult` where the timezone is already in hand.

**2. I found a decision the plan has to make, which neither of us had considered: the stale drop.** Changing location changes the weather, but today's looks were already composed for the old city and cached under Decision 5. Without handling it, you'd move Manila → Reykjavik and see outfits built for 26°C rain under a strip reading 12°C overcast.

Task 5 decides it: **changing location deletes today's drop so it rebuilds — and the rebuild is free.** Deleting the stored set is precisely what makes the next call a `drop` rather than a `regenerate`, and `MONETISATION.md` §2 says drops are never metered on any tier. You changed a setting; you didn't ask for a reroll. It also has to delete under the *new* timezone's local date, since moving across zones can change what "today" is.

Two things I deliberately kept out of scope, both noted in the plan: reverse geocoding (Open-Meteo has no endpoint, and a third-party one ships your coordinates off-stack — D8), and removing the Stylist's pill, which you already decided stays.

**1. Temporarily disable the ruleset, merge, re-enable** (recommended — leaves the rule intact afterwards):

# back it up first
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/rulesets/19622742 > /tmp/ruleset-backup.json

gh api -X PUT repos/:owner/:repo/rulesets/19622742 -f enforcement=disabled

content.text:
You're right, and I can name the defect precisely: it's a **card inside a card**. The picker was drawn as a floating dropdown that sits *over* the page on the Stylist — its own border, own background, own padding. Nested inside the Location row's card, you get two borders, two surfaces and an inner box floating with margin on all sides. It doesn't belong to the screen.

The extraction itself was right — one behaviour, one component, no drift. What I wrongly shared was the *presentation*.

Two ways to fix it, and they're genuinely different products:

**A. Inline, restyled.** The picker keeps expanding in place, but in Settings it renders with no surface of its own: full-width rows, hairline dividers, same rhythm as the toggles above it (`px-4 py-[15px]`), search field spanning the row, results as label-left / country-right rows — the item-detail spec-table language the README says to derive from. One component, a `variant` prop, behaviour identical.

**B. A bottom sheet.** Tapping Location opens a sheet, like Refine and Upgrade already do. The search field gets room, the results list gets height, and the keyboard has somewhere to go instead of squeezing a nested box. The project already has this pattern and STATE.md documents its z-index rule (`z-[60]`/`z-[70]` above the `z-50` nav).

**I'd take B.** A searchable list of variable length is exactly what a sheet is for, and on a phone the inline version will always feel cramped once four or five cities come back — the row grows, the page reflows under your thumb, and the field can end up under the keyboard. It also matches how you already reach for a picker elsewhere in the app. The cost is that the Stylist keeps its dropdown, so the two screens share the list and its behaviour but present it differently — which is honest, since one is a quick in-context correction and the other is a deliberate settings change.

Which do you want? If B, I'll also make the Stylist's dropdown a sheet later or leave it — separate call.

content.text:
Fixed and verified on device. 567 tests, tsc clean.

**What changed:**

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Header ate two-thirds of the sheet | Title 24px → 20px, body to a single muted line. `UpgradeSheet` earns that scale because it's making an argument; this is a control. |
| Search field was a box floating in the card | In `bare` mode it's now a row like the others — transparent, full width, hairline below. The card reads as one list. |
| Rows didn't share a rhythm | Both rows now use the same `px-4 py-[13px]` and hairline treatment. |

The screenshot confirms the sheet clears the bottom nav with the backdrop blur behind it — the `RefineSheet` failure mode, now pinned by a test that asserts `fixed`, `z-[70]`, and *not* `absolute`.

## Still needs your hands

Everything except the actual taps is verified. Three things I can't do (System Events is blocked, so I can't tap the Simulator):

1. **Open Location → search a city → pick it.** I'm watching `profiles` and will confirm the write, the `source: 'city'`, and the resolved timezone.
2. **Check the results list scrolls** rather than growing the sheet, once several cities come back. That's the whole reason it's a sheet.
3. **Then go to the Stylist** — it should show the new city with a drop rebuilt for that weather, recorded as a free `drop` and not a metered `regenerate`.

One thing worth flagging honestly: **`setLocation` has never executed.** Its pure helpers are tested (`locationColumns`, `locationChanged`, the GPS-suppression invariant), and the project has no precedent for testing Server Actions — but the action body itself, including the stale-drop deletion, is unexercised until you tap. That's the part I'd most want to see run.

Tap it when you're ready and I'll read the result.

content.text:
**Your test passes: the drop is free on the free tier.**

## Two bugs found by driving the real browser

Both were invisible to the test suite — 569 tests were green the whole time.

1. **City search showed results for an earlier keystroke.** Typing "Oslo" fires searches for "Os", "Osl", "Oslo", and whichever *resolved* last won. The list showed Oss and Os de Balaguer under a field reading Oslo. Fixed and re-verified live — "Oslo" now returns Oslo.

2. **The Stylist path doesn't clear the stale drop.** `setLocation` (Settings) clears it; `saveLocation` (the weather pill) doesn't. That's why your Zurich pick left Berlin's 16°C looks in place. **Not fixed yet** — and I want your call, because the fix isn't obvious.

## Why I stopped rather than fixing it

The naive fix breaks things. On the Stylist the order is: pick city → `generate` runs → `applyResult` calls `saveLocation`. If `saveLocation` cleared the drop, it would delete the looks `generate` had *just* stored, and the next load would regenerate — burning a model call every single time you switch city.

The correct fix is one level up: **`generate` should treat a changed location as invalidating today's stored set**, and rebuild instead of reading it. That's a change to the daily-drop logic itself (`lib/outfits/`, Decision 5 territory), not a two-line patch — which is why I'd rather you weigh in than have me quietly rewrite the generator's caching rule.

content.text:
**Fixed and proven live on both doors.**

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| **Settings** → Zurich → Oslo | drop cleared 3→0, rebuilt, `kind: drop` |
| **Stylist pill** → Oslo → Lisbon | looks rebuilt (names changed), weather now Lisbon 20° Clear, `kind: drop` |

Three `drop` events, **zero `regenerate`**, tier `free`. So on the free tier a location change costs nothing from your reroll allowance — through either entry point.

## Why the fix went in `generate`, not `saveLocation`

`saveLocation` runs inside `applyResult`, *after* `generate` has already stored the day's looks. Clearing there would delete what the same call just wrote, and every city switch would generate twice. So `generate` now skips the stored set when the requested location has moved and falls through — and the fall-through path already records a `drop` rather than a `regenerate`, so the rebuild is free by construction rather than by a special case.

## One judgement call I made, which you should sanity-check

**The threshold is 25km, and it's about weather rather than precision.** The Stylist's silent GPS refresh runs on every load, so a tighter bound would make anyone who commutes pay for a fresh generation every morning — while the forecast 10km away is the same forecast, so those looks were never actually wrong. Both doors now use one predicate (`locationMoved`), so they can't disagree about what counts as a move. `locationChanged` is deleted; it was superseded.

If you'd rather any deliberate city pick invalidate regardless of distance, that's a one-line change — but it would also mean GPS drift across a city boundary costs a generation.

**572 tests · tsc clean · build clean.**

Still outstanding from earlier: the **"1 Issue"** badge in the Next dev overlay that I spotted on `/settings` — I haven't looked at it yet, and I'd like to before this branch goes up for review.

content.text:
**Option B is better — invalidate on any deliberate pick, keep the distance rule only for GPS.**

The reason: distance is a *proxy* for intent, and it's the wrong proxy. What actually matters is whether the user asked.

- **A deliberate pick is a statement**: "give me looks for here." If they tap a city 10km away and nothing changes, the app looks broken and gives them no way to tell why. That's the worse failure — silent, and it makes the feature feel unreliable.
- **The GPS refresh is not a statement.** It runs on every load, in the background, and the user never asked for it. That's where the cost risk actually lives, and that's where a threshold belongs.

The 25km rule I shipped applies the same bar to both, which protects against the commute case but buys that protection by ignoring an explicit request.

Cost of switching: near zero. Deliberately picking a city under 25km away is rare, and when it happens the user wanted it.

Concretely, three cases:

| Situation | Signal | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Same place re-picked | rounded coords equal | do nothing — don't throw away today's looks for a no-op tap |
| Different place, deliberate | `source: "city"` | invalidate, rebuild as a free `drop` |
| Different place, GPS | `source: "geo"` | invalidate only past 25km |

The second row covers both the Settings sheet and the Stylist pill. The third covers the silent refresh *and* an explicit "Use my location" tap — which is fine, because if you tap it while standing still, nothing should change anyway.

One honest note: this brings back the "is it literally the same place" check I deleted an hour ago, for the first row. That's a small reversal, but it's load-bearing here — without it, tapping your own city costs you a regeneration.

Want me to switch it? It's a contained change to `locationMoved`'s callers plus tests.

git add -A && git commit -q -m "chore: drop a dead import left by the shared location payload" && git push -q origin feat/location-in-settings && gh pr create --title "feat: location in settings" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Adds a real location picker to `/settings`, driven by the same hook and option list the Stylist's weather pill uses, so the two entry points cannot drift.

## The constraint that shaped it

`saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value only exists as a by-product of `fetchForecast` during a generate — so today location is written as a side-effect of `applyResult`. Settings has no generate, and a null timezone falls back to UTC, which is exactly the failure Decision 5 exists to prevent (a UTC key rolls the daily drop over mid-evening).

So `setLocation` resolves the timezone first, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no API key, no AI, already cached 30 minutes per rounded coordinate. `saveLocation` deliberately does NOT gain that fetch — it already holds the timezone from the generate that just ran.

Both paths now write through `locationColumns`, so the column set cannot drift between them.

## A sheet, not an inline picker

The first attempt expanded the Stylist's picker inside the Location row and it read as a card inside a card — two borders, two backgrounds, an inner box floating in its own margin. That presentation was drawn for a control that floats *over* the page.

A sheet also fits what this is: a searchable list of unknown length. Inline, the row grows as results arrive and reflows the page under the user's thumb, and the field can end up beneath the keyboard. `RefineSheet` and `UpgradeSheet` already establish the pattern, and tests pin the failure mode `RefineSheet` shipped with — `fixed` not `absolute`, `z-[70]` above the `z-50` nav, nothing left in the tree when closed.

`LocationPicker` gains a `bare` variant that drops its own surface, so what differs between the two screens is presentation only — the behaviour, option markup and a11y semantics are shared. The Stylist keeps its dropdown, which is right: a quick in-context correction and a deliberate settings change are not the same gesture.

## The stale drop — the decision this PR exists to get right

Changing location changes the weather, and today's looks were composed for the old city. Decision 5 caches the drop; caching does not make a 26°C Manila outfit correct under a 12°C Reykjavik sky.

**A location change rebuilds the drop, and the rebuild is free.** `generation_events` records `kind` by whether a stored set already exists, so clearing it is precisely what makes the next call a `drop` rather than a metered `regenerate` — MONETISATION §2, drops are never metered on any tier. The user changed a setting; they did not ask for a reroll.

Two doors, two mechanisms, one predicate:

- **Settings** (`setLocation`) deletes the rows outright, keyed on the NEW timezone — crossing zones can change what "today" is, and deleting under the old key would destroy a past day's history while leaving the stale row untouched.
- **The Stylist** cannot do that: `saveLocation` runs *after* `generate` has stored the day's looks, so clearing there would delete what the same call just wrote and every city switch would generate twice. Instead `generate` skips the stored set when the requested location has moved, and falls through — a path that already records a `drop`.

**Intent decides, not distance.** Distance was only ever a proxy for intent, and the wrong one: someone who taps a city 10km away has asked for looks there, and a screen that does not change reads as broken. `invalidatesDrop` splits three cases — same place never rebuilds (a no-op re-tap is free), a deliberate pick always does however near, and a GPS fix only past 25km. That threshold belongs on GPS alone because the silent refresh runs on every load and nobody asked for it; a commuter must not pay for a generation each morning.

## Two bugs a real browser found that 569 green tests did not

- **City search showed results for an earlier keystroke.** Typing "Oslo" fires searches for "Os", "Osl", "Oslo", and whichever *resolved* last won — the list showed Oss and Os de Balaguer under a field reading Oslo. Responses are now accepted only while their query is still the latest, and clearing the field clears the results.
- **The Stylist path left stale looks in place**, described above.

## Verified live, in Chrome, on the free tier

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Settings: Zurich → Oslo | drop cleared 3→0, rebuilt, `kind: drop` |
| Stylist pill: Oslo → Lisbon | looks rebuilt, screen reads Lisbon 20° Clear, `kind: drop` |
| Stylist pill: Lisbon → Almada (~5km) | looks rebuilt — the case the distance rule alone would have ignored |
| `generation_events` where `kind='regenerate'` | **0** |

576 tests · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · lint unchanged from main's baseline.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

**PR #29 is open** — https://github.com/1curafu/Fitcheck/pull/29 — 10 commits, CI running. I'm watching it and will report the result.

## What's next

The queue after this merges, in order:

**#10 `wear-stats`** — the Wear Stats screen. Two warnings already recorded against it:
- **The plan has no gate.** It's Pro (`entitlements.analytics` / `.gapAnalysis`) and the plan predates the entitlements seam, so the gate has to be added.
- **Do NOT gate the item-detail wear tiles.** Times worn, cost-per-wear and last worn shipped free in PR #22 and you confirmed they stay. A fact about the piece you're looking at is free; the screen that analyses the whole wardrobe is Pro.
- It also carries an open design question I can't resolve alone: *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* is a **simulation** of what a hypothetical garment would enable, not a query. That needs designing before it can be built.

**#11 `styled-look-depth`** — three measured quality gaps in the styled look. Task 1 is independent and cheap: `diversify` is skipped on the styled shortlist, so the model picks between 20 variations of one idea.

**#12 `item-signals-in-generator`** — where `HOT_MATERIALS` finally dies and warmth reads material × texture.

## Two things I owe you that aren't in the queue

1. **The evening wear-confirmation plan.** You asked for it as its own plan after Settings; it's still unwritten. It replaces the rejected auto-log toggle and needs no push at all.
2. **The notifications/web-push plan** — the only thing that needs a service worker, and where the daily fit reminder lives.

## One caveat worth carrying forward

**CI has never passed on any of this.** #28 merged during the outage, so the run happening now on #29 is the first time `verify` sees a clean `npm ci` on Linux for either branch's code. If something environment-specific slipped through, it surfaces there — I'll tell you either way.

My suggestion: **#11 Task 1 next.** It's small, it's a visible quality win in a Pro feature, and it doesn't need a design decision first — unlike wear-stats, which is blocked on the gap-analysis question.

content.content:
# Styled Look Depth Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make "Style an outfit with this" as good as the daily drop. It currently returns one safe
look and then freezes for the rest of the day.

**Architecture:** No new machinery. Task 1 reuses `diversify`, which the daily path already calls and
the styled path does not. Tasks 2–4 widen the styled look from one to a small set and add an explicit
"try another", metered through the ledger that queue #8 builds.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js 16 App Router, Supabase, Vitest.

## Why this exists

Written 2026-07-31, after PR #22 shipped the feature and the user asked whether the styled look is
"generating a new outfit set or not so good as it can be". It generates a genuinely new outfit — it
rebuilds from the whole closet with the piece pinned, it does not filter today's looks — but three
things hold it below the daily drop. All three were confirmed against the merged code, not assumed.

## ⚠️ Read before writing anything — what is ALREADY decided elsewhere

This plan was written *after* checking the rest of the queue, specifically so it does not re-decide
things other plans own. Do not relitigate these:

| Question | Already answered by | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| Is styling free or paid? | `MONETISATION.md:87` | On the **meter**; unlimited on Pro. Pro feature #2. |
| Where does the meter live? | `todo/2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` (queue #8) | `generation_events`, an append-only ledger. `assertCanGenerate` is the seam and `style-actions.ts` already calls it. |
| Is "limited" an error? | queue #8 | **No — a first-class status.** `StyleCta` already renders a `limited` state; PR #22 built it that way deliberately. |
| Should Decision 5 forbid this? | `done/2026-07-24-item-detail-rebuild.md` | No. Decision 5 forbids paying twice for the *same* question; styling a chosen piece is a different question, so it gets its own cached answer. |

**Sequencing:** Task 1 is independent and can ship on its own at any time. **Tasks 2–4 must come after
queue #8**, because they spend the meter that plan defines. Executing them earlier means inventing a
second counting scheme, which is exactly what queue #8 exists to prevent.

**A defect in queue #8 that this plan depends on:** `generation_events.is_regenerate` is a boolean, and
a styled generation is neither the day's free drop for an occasion (`false` would mark that occasion as
already dropped) nor a regenerate of one (`true` would make styling eat the regenerate allowance). A
note has been added to that plan's schema to replace the boolean with `kind text` —
`'drop' | 'regenerate' | 'styled'`. **If it is still a boolean when you get here, fix it there, not
here.**

## Source

`design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html:587-657` (item detail). Feature as shipped:
`app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts`, `components/closet/style-cta.tsx`, `lib/outfits/styled.ts`,
`lib/outfits/styled-store.ts`.

## File structure

| File | Responsibility | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts` | Diversify the shortlist; return a set; honour "try another" | Modify |
| `lib/outfits/styled-store.ts` | Load/save a SET of styled looks | Modify |
| `lib/outfits/styled.ts` | Pure helpers | Modify |
| `components/closet/style-cta.tsx` | Index tabs + "try another" | Modify |
| `supabase/migrations/*_styled_look_index.sql` | Allow >1 styled look per item per day | **Create** (Task 2) |

---

### Task 1: Diversify the styled shortlist — independent, ship any time

**Files:** Modify `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts`; append to `lib/outfits/__tests__/styled.test.ts`

The daily path does `diversify(ranked, 20)` before the model sees anything; the styled path does
`pinned.slice(0, 20)`. Ranking **clusters** — a neutral top harmonises with everything, so the raw top
20 are near-identical and the model is choosing between 20 variations of one idea. This is the same
reasoning that produced `lib/generator/diversity.ts` in PR #14/#15; it was simply never applied to the
second consumer.

/**
 * The shortlist handed to the re-ranker for a styled look.
 *
 * The daily path calls `diversify` before the model sees anything; this path
 * shipped with `pinned.slice(0, 20)` and never got it. Ranking CLUSTERS — a
 * neutral top harmonises with everything, so the raw top of a pinned list is
 * near-identical and the model ends up choosing between twenty variations of
 * one idea, then returning the safest.
 *
 * Same reasoning that produced `lib/generator/diversity.ts` in PR #14/#15,
 * applied to the second consumer. `diversify` TIERS rather than filters, so
 * nothing is discarded and a closet too small to diversify still yields every
 * candidate — the collapse PR #15 fixed on the daily path cannot reappear here.
 *
 * It only reorders a list `pinItem` already filtered, so every combo still
 * contains the pinned piece.
 */
export function shortlistFor<T extends { items: { id: string; category: string }[]; score: number }>(
  pinned: T[],
  n = 20,
): T[] {
  return diversify(pinned, n);
}

content.text:
I need to stop and report a finding rather than ship this.

## Task 1 fixes a problem that doesn't exist

I measured it four ways before believing it. **`diversify` cannot improve a pinned shortlist**, in any closet shape I can construct:

| Closet | pinned combos | Truncated? | Distinct bottoms/shoes BEFORE → AFTER |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your real 21-item | 6 | no | 6/3 → **6/3** |
| 50 pieces (free cap) | 13 | no | 13/13 → **13/13** |
| 38 pieces, 25 bottoms | 25 | **yes** | 20/10 → **20/10** |
| 82 pieces, 40 bottoms | 40 | **yes** | 20/20 → **20/20** |

Identical every time — including the cases where `slice(0, 20)` genuinely truncates.

**Two reasons, both structural:**

1. **`pinned` is almost never longer than 20.** Pinning one garment yields at most `max(#bottoms, #shoes)` combos, because `buildCandidates`' breadth-first walk emits each top once per pass. You'd need 21+ bottoms *or* 21+ shoes before the slice removed anything at all.

2. **Even when it does truncate, there's nothing to reorder.** That same walk already pairs each pass with a different bottom and shoe — the pinned list arrives maximally varied. And `diversify` tiers on *top + bottom* freshness; when you pin a top, every combo shares it, so the tiering collapses to "sort by bottom", which the walk already did.

So the plan's premise — *"the model is choosing between 20 variations of one idea"* — is true of the **daily** path, where the list spans many tops and ranking clusters across them. Pinning collapses exactly that. The README's "cheap real quality win" is wrong, and my own passing tests only prove it on a hand-built ranked list that `buildCandidates` cannot actually produce.

**I haven't committed anything.**

## What I'd do instead

Drop Task 1 and record why in the plan, then go to **Task 3** — *"cached all day with no way to ask for another"*. That's where the "not as good as it can be" feeling you originally reported actually comes from: you tap a second time and the identical look returns with no explanation, while the stylist screen has a visible Regenerate for precisely that situation. Task 2 (one look → two) is the other half.

Both need the ledger, and **queue #8's `kind` column already exists** — it shipped in PR #25 with `'drop' | 'regenerate' | 'styled'`. So the dependency the plan was waiting on is satisfied; Tasks 2–4 are unblocked now.

Your call: drop Task 1, or keep it anyway as consistency insurance in case `buildCandidates` ever changes shape?

**Can it destroy anything? No, and that's structural.** `diversify` returns `[...tier1, ...tier2, ...tier3].slice(0, n)` — a *permutation* of its input, capped at the same 20. input.content:
-- A styling returns a SET of looks, not one.
--
-- `outfits_styled_unique (user_id, styled_item_id, generated_on)` allowed exactly
-- one row per piece per local day, which is what bounded a styling to a single
-- look. Widening it needs an ordinal.
--
-- ⚠️ That ordinal is NOT `look_index`, and this is the trap worth reading.
-- Styled rows keep `look_index` NULL on purpose: `outfits_daily_unique` covers
-- (user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index), and Postgres treats NULLs as
-- distinct, which is the only reason a styled look and the day's drop can share
-- an occasion without colliding. Giving styled rows a real `look_index` would
-- reintroduce that collision — a styled look at index 0 for `work` today would
-- clash with the drop's look 0. So the order lives in its own column.
alter table public.outfits
  add column if not exists styled_index smallint;

-- Existing styled rows are the first look of their set.
update public.outfits
  set styled_index = 0
  where styled_item_id is not null and styled_index is null;

drop index if exists outfits_styled_unique;

create unique index outfits_styled_unique
  on public.outfits (user_id, styled_item_id, generated_on, styled_index)
  where styled_item_id is not null;

content.text:
**Cache hit confirmed** — `styled` events stayed at 2, rows stayed at 2, and the look opened in ~3s versus ~16s cold. No model call.

But this exposed a real defect in my own Task 3 work:

**"Try another look" is unreachable.** Tapping the primary navigates straight to `/outfits/[id]`, so the button I put below it on the item-detail screen is never seen — and coming back remounts the component, resetting `styled` to `false`. It can literally never appear.

The fix is to derive it from the server, not from session state:

  ).length > 0;""",
"""  const styledToday = (await loadStyledLooks(user.id, item.id, today)).length > 0;""")
s = s.replace('import { localDateFor } from "@/lib/outfits/local-date";',
              'import { localDateFor } from "@/lib/outfits/local-date";\nimport { loadStyledLooks } from "@/lib/outfits/styled-store";')
open(p,"w").write(s)

# 2. ItemDetail forwards it.
p = "components/closet/item-detail.tsx"
s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace("styleCta={<StyleCta itemId={item.id} />}", "styleCta={<StyleCta itemId={item.id} styledToday={styledToday} />}")

content.text:
Both plans written and queued as **#12a** and **#12b**. Also: **PR #30's CI passed** — `verify` green in 1m32s, mergeable.

## The wear-confirmation plan (#12a)

Buildable now, no push needed. But it has **a dependency neither of us had spotted**: nothing in the app records that a look was *opened*. `outfits` has no `viewed_at` and nothing writes one — so the rule you set ("it asks only about looks actually opened") can't be implemented without adding it. That's the plan's one schema change, and it comes with a trap: the write must happen from the client on mount, **not** in the Server Component's render, or it fires for prefetches the user never sees.

Both of your rules are encoded as tests rather than prose — Yes/No must have identical styling, and there's a test asserting no dismiss/close/skip control exists at all, because that's the lone-Yes problem wearing a different hat.

**One question I left open rather than deciding:** what a backdrop tap does. My recommendation is that it closes for the session *without* setting `askedOn`, so a mis-tap doesn't silently consume the day's question.

## The notifications plan (#12b)

Two things you should know before this ever gets scheduled.

**The design promises more than a reminder.** `Fitcheck.dc.html:1383` reads *"Tomorrow's weather + a planned look"* — a *planned look* means generating an outfit per subscriber per night, pushed rather than pulled. That's roughly **$90/month per 1000 subscribed users**, against **~$0** for weather alone. It also pre-commits the stylist before the user has said what the day is, which the smart-default work treats as a prediction on purpose. I recommend weather-only and flagged it as **blocking** — it's your money and your product call, not the implementer's.

**iOS is the harder constraint.** Push reaches only home-screen-installed PWAs. Most of your users are iPhone users in a Safari tab, and for them nothing will ever arrive. The plan makes the toggle explain installing rather than render a switch that's on and silent — which is exactly why it was cut from Settings rather than shipped inert.

Two smaller things it pins: the cron route must authenticate (`CRON_SECRET`), because an open one is a public endpoint that pushes to your whole userbase; and it's the first server-side code to run as service role, where RLS doesn't protect you and every query has to scope `user_id` itself.

Also left open: whether the reminder hour is user-chosen, and whether this is free or Pro — `MONETISATION.md` doesn't tier it, though free is the consistent answer since it drives the habit loop that §3 says creates a payer.

**PR #30 is ready to merge whenever you are.**

# Usage & Pricing for Cron Jobs

> **🔒 Permissions Required**: Cron Jobs

Cron jobs invoke [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions). This means the same [usage](/docs/limits) and [pricing](/pricing) limits will apply.

|                | **Number of cron jobs per project** | **Minimum interval** | **Scheduling precision** |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------ |
| **Hobby**      | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per day         | Per-hour (±59 min)       |
| **Pro**        | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per minute      | Per-minute               |
| **Enterprise** | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per minute      | Per-minute               |

### Hobby scheduling limits

> **💡 Note:** Hobby accounts are limited to cron jobs that run **once per day**. Cron
> expressions that would run more frequently will fail during deployment.

Hobby plans have two restrictions on cron jobs:

1. **Daily execution limit**: Cron jobs can only run once per day. Expressions like `0 * * * *` (per-hour) or `*/30 * * * *` (every 30 minutes) will fail deployment with the error:
   *Hobby accounts are limited to daily cron jobs. This cron expression would run more than once per day.*

2. **Timing precision**: Vercel cannot assure a timely cron job invocation. For example, a cron job configured as `0 1 * * *` (every day at 1 am) will trigger anywhere between 1:00 am and 1:59 am.

For cron jobs that run more frequently or with precise timing, **upgrade to our [Pro](/docs/plans/pro-plan) plan**.

## Pricing

Cron jobs are included in **all plans**.

You use a function to invoke a cron job, and therefore [usage](/docs/limits) and [pricing](/pricing) limits for these functions apply to all cron job executions:

- [Functions limits and pricing](/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing)

content.text:
Verified, and it's a real trap in the plan I just wrote.

## What's free

**The push itself costs nothing.** FCM, APNs and Mozilla's autopush are run by the browser vendors at no charge — there's no per-message fee for web push, at any volume. VAPID keys are self-generated, `web-push` is open source, and the subscriptions table is a rounding error on Supabase.

## What actually costs money

**1. The scheduler — and my plan wouldn't have deployed.** Vercel's docs are explicit:

> **Hobby accounts are limited to cron jobs that run once per day.** Cron expressions that would run more frequently will **fail during deployment.**

My plan specifies `0 * * * *` (hourly), which is exactly the example they give as failing. And Hobby's scheduling precision is **±59 minutes**, so even a daily cron fires anywhere inside an hour — useless for "remind me at 07:00".

Hourly granularity isn't optional here: users are in different timezones, so you need to check every hour who's at their local 7am. That means **Vercel Pro, $20/month**.

**2. Option B's pre-generated looks** — ~$90/month per 1000 subscribers, as before.

## But the $20 is avoidable

The scheduler doesn't have to be Vercel:

- **Supabase `pg_cron` + `pg_net`** — included free, runs on any interval, calls your route handler. You're already on Supabase, and this keeps the trigger next to the data it reads.
- **GitHub Actions on a schedule** — free for public repos, and this repo is public. A 3-line workflow curling the endpoint with the secret.

So the honest total for a weather-only reminder is **€0/month**, provided the cron doesn't run on Vercel Hobby.

Recorded in the plan and the README, so this isn't rediscovered later.

**Short answer to your question: no, push itself is free.** The only mandatory spend would have been $20/month for Vercel Pro to get an hourly cron — and that's sidestepped entirely with Supabase `pg_cron`, which you already have.

Which makes the economics of this feature better than I implied earlier. It doesn't change your decision to defer it, though — the blocker was never cost, it's that most of your users are in a Safari tab where nothing gets delivered. That's still true.

Worth noting the finding has value beyond this plan: **`0 * * * *` fails at *deploy* on Vercel Hobby**, and Hobby crons drift by up to 59 minutes. Anything scheduled you build later — a cleanup job, a digest, the occasion learner — hits the same wall, so Supabase `pg_cron` is probably the default scheduler for this project rather than a workaround for one feature.

Back to where we were: **PR #30 is green and mergeable**, and **#12a wear-confirmation** is the next buildable thing — now the only nudge mechanism you have, since push is parked.

content.content:
# Open-Meteo Free Tier and Commercial Use

## Commercial Use Policy

The free API tier is **not permitted for commercial use**. According to the pricing page: "The free API is for non-commercial use, rate-limited to 10,000 calls/day, and carries no uptime guarantee."

## Free Tier Limits

The free tier has three rate restrictions:
- **Minutely**: 600 calls/minute
- **Hourly**: 5,000 calls/hour
- **Daily**: 10,000 calls/day
- **Monthly**: 300,000 calls/month

## Paid Plans

The page does not display specific pricing amounts. It outlines three commercial tiers:
- **Standard**: 1M calls/month
- **Professional**: 5M calls/month
- **Enterprise**: 50M+ calls/month

To see actual prices, users must click on a plan to proceed through Stripe checkout.

## Licensing Requirements

Open-Meteo data falls under "Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)," which "mandates giving appropriate credit and indicating any modifications made to the data." This applies to all use cases, including commercial applications on paid plans.

p = "docs/MONETISATION.md"

s = s.replace("""## 7. Open questions""",
"""## 7. What a break-even model needs, and what this document was missing

_Added 2026-08-12, when a break-even model was first asked for._

**Sections 1–4 model COST-TO-SERVE, not a business.** They answer "what does an AI generation cost", and
they answer it well and by measurement. A break-even model needs three more things this document did not
have: what actually reaches the bank from €5, the infrastructure that is not AI, and the fixed costs
that exist whether anyone subscribes or not.

### 7.1 €5 is not €5 — roughly €3.84 reaches us

Verified against Stripe's published EEA pricing, 2026-08-12:

| Line | On a €5/mo subscription |
|---|---|
| Gross | €5.00 |
| **VAT** (EU digital services, OSS — 19% DE, 17% LU … 27% HU) | **−€0.80** if the price is VAT-INCLUSIVE |
| **Stripe**, EEA standard card — 1.5% + €0.25 | −€0.33 |
| **Stripe Billing** — 0.7% of volume | −€0.04 |
| **Net** | **≈ €3.84** |

That is a **23% haircut**, and two things inside it deserve attention:

- **The €0.25 fixed fee is 5% on its own at this price**, before any percentage applies. It is the
  single strongest argument for the annual plan §7.2 lists as undecided: at €48/yr the same fixed fee is
  0.5%, and net rises from ~€3.84×12 = €46 to about €51.
- **A premium (rewards/business) card costs 2.8% + €0.25, not 1.5%** — a mix assumption, not a constant.
- ⚠️ **Whether €5 is VAT-inclusive or exclusive is not decided anywhere.** If exclusive, a German
  customer pays €5.95 and roughly €4.58 reaches us. This single unstated choice moves net revenue ~19%.

### 7.2 Infrastructure this document never counted

| Cost | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Open-Meteo** | ⚠️ **LICENSING EXPOSURE** | The free API is **not permitted for commercial use** — verified 2026-08-12. `CLAUDE.md` records it as "free, no key", which was true while nothing was sold. Weather is on the critical path of every generate. A paid tier is required the day Pro is charged for, and CC BY 4.0 attribution is mandatory in the app regardless. |
| **Supabase egress** | **Not counted, likely dominant** | §2 measured STORAGE (330 kB/item) but never bandwidth. Every closet screen, flat-lay and diary cell serves cutouts through signed URLs, so egress scales with *engagement*, not just library size — and egress is the metered line, not gigabytes at rest. **This needs measuring before any model is trusted.** |
| **Supabase plan** | Not counted | Free tier caps DB, storage, egress and MAU; Pro is $25/mo plus usage. |
| **Vercel** | Not counted | ⚠️ Hobby is **non-commercial only**, so a paid product needs Pro at **$20/mo**. That also removes the cron restriction recorded in `plans/scoping/2026-08-11-notifications.md`. |
| **Domain** | Not counted | ~€12/yr. |
| **App store commission** | Not counted, future | If Capacitor ships (Phase 4+), Apple requires In-App Purchase for a digital subscription: **15% under the Small Business Program, otherwise 30%** — replacing Stripe's ~7%, not adding to it. Verify current terms before committing; it changes the price you must charge to net the same. |

### 7.3 The shape of the model

```
Break-even subscribers  =  fixed monthly costs
                           ─────────────────────────────────────────
                           net revenue/Pro − (cost to serve 1 Pro
                                              + free users per Pro
                                                × cost to serve 1 free)
```

Everything on the right except *fixed monthly costs* and *free users per Pro* is measurable today. The
two unmeasured inputs are **Supabase egress per active user** and the **Open-Meteo commercial tier**.

**Worked illustration — not a forecast, and not advice.** Using this document's own measured figures
(free ≈ $0.14/mo AI, Pro ≈ $0.90/mo heavy), €3.84 net, fixed costs of Vercel $20 + Supabase $25 + domain
≈ **$46/mo**, and §2's 5% conversion (so 19 free users per Pro):

```
contribution per Pro ≈ 3.84 − (0.90 + 19 × 0.14) ≈ €0.28
break-even ≈ 46 / 0.28 ≈ 164 Pro subscribers ≈ 3,300 total users
```

⚠️ **That €0.28 is razor-thin and is the real finding.** It is dominated by the *free* users each payer
carries, not by the payer. Three levers move it far more than price does: conversion rate (halve the
free-per-Pro ratio and contribution roughly doubles), free-tier AI usage (§2 already says *"if real usage
runs above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price"* —
that sentence is now load-bearing), and annual billing (§7.1). Egress, once measured, can only push it
down.

**Do not treat the number as a plan.** It omits the two unmeasured inputs above, assumes every card is
an EEA standard card, and assumes 5% conversion, which is an aspiration rather than an observation.

The cheap combination is near-free after a one-time build; the expensive one scales with closet size *and* engagement, which is the exact shape §2 rejected for styled looks.

## Now the honest answer: no, that was not all

`MONETISATION.md` modelled **cost-to-serve**, not a business. Three things were missing, and two are material.

**1. €5 is not €5 — about €3.84 reaches you.** Verified against Stripe's published EEA pricing today: VAT (19% DE, if the price is VAT-inclusive) −€0.80, Stripe 1.5% + €0.25 −€0.33, Stripe Billing 0.7% −€0.04. A **23% haircut**. Note the €0.25 fixed fee is **5% on its own** at this price — which turns "annual pricing, not decided" into a decision worth ~€5/subscriber/year. And whether €5 is VAT-inclusive or exclusive isn't written down anywhere; it moves net revenue ~19%.

**2. ⚠️ Open-Meteo's free API is not permitted for commercial use.** `CLAUDE.md` records it as "free, no key" — true while nothing was sold. Weather is on the critical path of *every* generate, so a paid tier is required the day you charge for Pro. CC BY 4.0 attribution is mandatory regardless. This is a licensing exposure, not just a cost line.

**3. Supabase egress was never counted, and is probably the dominant infra cost.** §2 measured storage at rest (330 kB/item) but not bandwidth. Every closet grid, flat-lay and diary cell serves cutouts through signed URLs, so egress scales with *engagement*, not library size. Also uncounted: Supabase Pro ($25/mo), and **Vercel Hobby is non-commercial only** so a paid product needs Pro ($20/mo).

## The finding that should shape your model

Working it through with the doc's own measured numbers — €46/mo fixed, €3.84 net, 5% conversion:

```
contribution per Pro ≈ 3.84 − (0.90 + 19 × 0.14) ≈ €0.28
break-even ≈ 164 Pro ≈ 3,300 total users
```

**That €0.28 is razor-thin, and it's dominated by the 19 free users each payer carries — not by the payer.** Price is the weakest lever you have. Conversion rate, free-tier AI usage, and annual billing all move it far more. It also means §2's existing line — *"if real usage runs above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price"* — is now load-bearing rather than a footnote.

**Treat that number as a shape, not a forecast.** It assumes 5% conversion (an aspiration, not an observation), assumes every card is an EEA standard card, and omits the two things still unmeasured: egress per active user, and the Open-Meteo commercial tier. I'd measure egress before trusting any model — it's the one input that can only push contribution down.

I'm not a licensed advisor and this is cost arithmetic rather than financial advice — the assumptions are all stated in §7.3 so you can swap your own in.
